lesson.title: Sufficiency, Factorisation and Minimal Sufficiency
objectives: Prove an instance of sufficiency on a coin, from counting and cancellation alone.
Read a joint density as a likelihood, and say why θ-free factors may be discarded.
Apply the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem, naming both of its conditions.
Give the sufficient statistic for the Bernoulli, Poisson, exponential, normal and Uniform families.
Establish minimal sufficiency by the ratio criterion, and let the criterion produce the statistic.
Recognise which of the three standard phrasings a question is using, and do the matching work.
Say which transformations preserve sufficiency, and what is and is not unique.
Relate sufficiency to completeness, to Rao–Blackwell and to the MLE, and state what does not follow.
traps: For Uniform(0, θ) the sufficient statistic is the maximum, not Σxᵢ.
With σ² unknown the normal needs (Σxᵢ, Σxᵢ²); only with σ² known does Σxᵢ suffice.
A minimal sufficient statistic is not unique; the partition it induces is.
Only one-to-one functions of a sufficient statistic are guaranteed sufficient.
A complete sufficient statistic is minimal sufficient, but minimal sufficiency does not imply completeness.
The dimension of a minimal sufficient statistic can exceed the dimension of the parameter — Uniform(θ, θ+1).
The Cauchy location family reduces no further than the order statistics.
Sufficiency is relative to the model: changing what is known changes the statistic, with the data unchanged.
A sufficient statistic need not be an estimator of θ, and need not be unbiased or low-variance.

lesson.title: Completeness, Exponential Families, Ancillarity and Basu
objectives: State completeness as a property of a family of distributions, and say why it is not a property of a statistic on its own.
Prove a statistic complete by the standard route: set E[g(T)] = 0, and use uniqueness of a power series, a polynomial or an integral.
Read completeness off the exponential-family form, and recognise a curved family where that argument fails.
Identify an ancillary statistic and apply Basu's theorem to get independence without touching a joint density.
Disprove completeness by constructing a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero.
Keep sufficient, minimal, complete and ancillary apart — the exam tests the boundaries, not the definitions.
traps: Calling a statistic complete without naming the family it is complete for.
Assuming minimal sufficient implies complete — curved families are the counterexample.
Applying the exponential-family criterion to a family whose support moves with θ.
Forgetting that the natural parameter space must contain an open rectangle, not just two or three points.
Using Basu without checking that T is complete as well as sufficient.
Treating 'ancillary' as 'useless' — an ancillary statistic is exactly what Basu needs, and it can still matter when you condition.
Proving E[g(T)] = 0 for one θ and concluding completeness. It must hold for every θ in Θ.

lesson.title: Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé
objectives: State Rao–Blackwell and say why the statistic conditioned on must be sufficient.
Compute E[δ(X) | T = t] in the standard cases, using the conditional distribution of the sample given its total.
State Lehmann–Scheffé and explain exactly which word turns 'an improvement' into 'the unique best'.
Produce a UMVUE by either route — Rao–Blackwellise a crude unbiased estimator, or find an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic directly.
Say when a UMVUE fails to exist, and when it exists but is absurd.
Separate the UMVUE from the MLE, and know which of the two survives a change of parameter.
traps: Conditioning on a statistic that is not sufficient, and producing an 'estimator' that still contains θ.
Reading Rao–Blackwell as a strict improvement. It is ≤, with equality when δ was already a function of T.
Claiming uniqueness from Rao–Blackwell alone. Uniqueness needs completeness.
Applying Lehmann–Scheffé in a curved family, where no complete sufficient statistic exists.
Squaring the UMVUE of θ and calling it the UMVUE of θ². That is MLE invariance, and UMVUEs do not have it.
Assuming the UMVUE must beat the MLE on mean squared error. For the normal variance it does not.
Forgetting to subtract the bias term: x̄² estimates μ² + σ²/n, not μ².

lesson.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
objectives: Build the likelihood of a sample and say why it is a function of θ, not of x.
Derive an MLE through the log-likelihood and the score equation, and verify it is a maximum.
Recognise when the derivative method fails and the maximum sits on a boundary.
Use invariance to get the MLE of a function of θ without redoing the work.
Separate 'maximum likelihood' from 'unbiased', and state the properties the MLE does have.
traps: Writing L(θ) and then differentiating with respect to x.
Maximising L instead of ℓ, and drowning in the product rule.
Setting the derivative to zero when the support depends on θ.
Forgetting the second-order check, so a minimum or a stationary point is reported as the MLE.
Re-deriving from scratch for g(θ) when invariance gives it in one line.
Assuming the MLE is unbiased, or that it must equal the UMVUE.
Dividing by n−1 in σ̂² because that is the formula you have written a hundred times.

topics.name: Method of moments, minimum chi-square, least squares

lesson.title: Method of Moments, Minimum Chi-square and Least Squares
objectives: Set up and solve the moment equations for a one- or two-parameter family, choosing raw or central moments to keep the algebra short.
State what the method of moments guarantees (consistency, asymptotic normality) and what it does not (unbiasedness, efficiency, a legal estimate).
Recognise the two families the exam uses against the method: U(a,b), where the estimate can be impossible, and Cauchy, where there is no moment to match.
Define the minimum chi-square and modified minimum chi-square estimators, and say what data they need.
Derive the least squares normal equations as moment conditions, and see least squares as one more instance of the same idea.
traps: The divisor in σ̃² is n, not n−1.
θ̃ = 2x̄ for U(0,θ) can be less than x₍ₙ₎, and then it is not an estimate at all.
Consistency does not imply unbiasedness.
No moments, no method — the Cauchy has no mean.
Least squares needs no normality; it only coincides with ML when the errors are normal.

lesson.title: The Cramér–Rao Bound and Fisher Information
objectives: Compute Fisher information by either formula, E[(∂ℓ/∂θ)²] or −E[∂²ℓ/∂θ²], and scale it to a sample as nI₁(θ).
Write the Cramér–Rao bound for an unbiased estimator of θ, and for a function g(θ) with [g′(θ)]² on top.
Check the regularity conditions before quoting the bound, and name the family where they fail.
Decide whether a given estimator attains the bound, using the linear-score condition rather than guesswork.
Compute efficiency and relative efficiency, and state what the bound says about the MLE as n grows.
traps: Quoting the bound for a family whose support moves with θ.
Forgetting the [g′(θ)]² numerator when the target is a function of θ rather than θ itself.
Using the bound on a biased estimator without the (1 + b′(θ))² numerator.
Writing I₁(θ) where the question wants nI₁(θ), or the reverse.
Assuming a UMVUE must attain the bound — it need not.
Confusing observed information −∂²ℓ/∂θ² at θ̂ with expected information −E[∂²ℓ/∂θ²].
Treating 'the MLE is efficient' as a finite-sample statement. It is asymptotic.

lesson.title: Bayesian Estimation and Conjugate Priors
objectives: Write a posterior as proportional to prior times likelihood and recognise the resulting kernel.
State and apply the Beta–Binomial, Gamma–Poisson, Gamma–Exponential and Normal–Normal conjugate updates.
Express a posterior mean as a weighted average of the prior mean and the MLE, and give the weight.
Give the Bayes estimator under squared-error, absolute-error and 0–1 loss, and say when they differ.
Construct a credible interval and distinguish its interpretation from that of a confidence interval.
State Jeffreys' prior, compute it for a Bernoulli probability, and say what an improper prior requires.
traps: Gamma–Poisson adds Σx to the shape; Gamma–Exponential adds n to the shape. They are reversed.
A uniform prior equates the posterior MODE with the MLE, not the posterior mean.
Jeffreys' prior for a Bernoulli probability is Beta(½, ½), not the uniform prior.
Precisions add in the Normal–Normal update; variances do not.
The second Beta parameter takes the failures, n − x, not n.
A credible interval is a probability statement about θ; a confidence interval is not.
Mean, median and mode of a posterior differ unless it is symmetric, and the loss decides which to report.
'The Bayes estimator' is undefined until a loss function is named.

topics.name: Decision theory: loss, risk, admissibility, minimax

lesson.title: Decision Theory: Loss, Risk, Admissibility and Minimax
objectives: Define loss, decision rule, risk and Bayes risk, and say which are functions of θ and which are numbers.
Decide whether one rule dominates another, and hence whether a rule is admissible.
Define the minimax criterion and compute a minimax value by flattening a risk curve.
Apply the three relations between Bayes, minimax and admissible rules, and state what does not follow.
Derive the minimax estimator of a binomial proportion and identify the least favourable prior.
Translate a testing problem into decision-theoretic language and say why Neyman–Pearson is not minimax.
traps: Risk is a function of θ; Bayes risk and the minimax value are the numbers derived from it.
Admissible does not imply minimax, and minimax does not imply admissible without uniqueness.
A Bayes rule is minimax only if its risk is constant — and constant risk alone is not sufficient either.
A rule that ignores the data entirely is admissible, which is what makes admissibility weak.
The MLE of a normal mean vector is inadmissible for dimension three or more, by James–Stein.
Neyman–Pearson constrains the size and maximises power; it does not minimise the maximum error probability.
Under squared-error loss, risk includes the squared bias, so a biased rule's variance is not its risk.
For weighted absolute loss the Bayes rule is a quantile, not the median, and it moves away from the costlier error.

topics.name: Neyman–Pearson, MLR, UMP, when UMP fails

lesson.title: Neyman–Pearson, Monotone Likelihood Ratio and UMP Tests
objectives: State the Neyman–Pearson lemma and use the likelihood ratio to find the most powerful test of one simple hypothesis against another.
Turn 'reject when the ratio is large' into an explicit critical region, and fix the constant from the size condition.
Recognise a monotone likelihood ratio family and quote Karlin–Rubin to get a UMP test for a one-sided alternative.
Say exactly why no UMP test exists for a two-sided alternative, and name what is used instead.
Compute size and power for a given test, and read a power function.
traps: The critical value never contains μ₁.
MLR gives one-sided UMP only.
Discrete data may need randomisation to hit size α exactly.
Power is computed under H₁, size under H₀.

lesson.title: The Likelihood Ratio Test and Wilks' Theorem
objectives: Write the likelihood ratio statistic with the correct sets in the numerator and denominator, and justify its range 0 < λ ≤ 1.
Carry out both maximisations, including the case where a nuisance parameter must be re-estimated under the null.
Derive the three standard normal results: the z test, the t test, and the two-tailed region on Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².
State Wilks' theorem with its degrees of freedom and its regularity conditions, and say why the statistic is −2 log λ.
Count degrees of freedom correctly for multinomial nulls, equality-of-means nulls, and nulls with nuisance parameters.
Place the test against Neyman–Pearson, and state its invariance and sufficiency properties.
traps: The denominator maximises over the WHOLE space Θ, not over the alternative Θ₁.
The range is 0 < λ ≤ 1; '0 < λ < ∞' is false.
−2 log λ is asymptotically chi-square, never standard normal — it cannot be negative.
A null that is silent about a parameter leaves it free, so re-estimate it under the restriction.
A multinomial with k categories has k − 1 free parameters, not k.
'k means are all equal' is k − 1 independent restrictions, not k.
Nuisance parameters unknown under both hypotheses add nothing to the degrees of freedom.
The MLE of a normal variance divides by n, not n − 1.

lesson.title: The Sequential Probability Ratio Test
objectives: State the SPRT procedure and say what it fixes in advance and what it leaves free.
Compute Wald's boundary constants A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α) and their logarithms.
Derive the two parallel boundary lines for Bernoulli data and identify the slope and intercepts.
Run the test on a given sequence and find the stopping point.
Define the OC function and the ASN, and compute the ASN at both hypotheses by Wald's formula.
State the Wald–Wolfowitz optimality property and the method's limitations, including α' + β' ≤ α + β.
traps: Both α and β are fixed; the SAMPLE SIZE is the random quantity.
A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α) — both error rates appear in both constants.
The slope of the boundary lines comes from the hypotheses; the intercepts carry the error rates.
The slope is −v/k, and the minus sign matters — v is negative.
Both ASN values must come out positive; E₀[Z] is negative and E₁[Z] positive.
The ASN is largest BETWEEN the hypotheses, so neither E(N|H₀) nor E(N|H₁) is the worst case.
Simple against simple only.
The true error rates are not exactly α and β; α' + β' ≤ α + β.

lesson.title: Size and Power of a Test
objectives: Compute the size of a given test by evaluating its rejection region under the null value.
Compute the power of a given test at a stated alternative, for discrete, flat-density and normal models.
Read and sketch a power function, and use the fact that its value at the null equals the size.
Find the size of a test with a composite null, and say why the worst case sits at the boundary.
Solve the sample-size problem: given α and a required power at a stated alternative, find the smallest n.
Say which changes raise power at no cost and which only trade one error against the other.
traps: The power is computed under the alternative; only the size uses the null.
'More than 3' means 4 or more — one word moves the answer.
A composite null takes its size at the boundary, not at an interior value.
A two-sided test's power is a sum over both tails, and is lower than the one-sided test's at the same alternative.
Sample size rounds UP; power rises with √n, not n.
β means the Type II error rate in some books and the power function in others — never write it bare.

lesson.title: Confidence Intervals and Pivotal Quantities
objectives: Define a pivotal quantity and decide whether a proposed quantity is one.
Construct a confidence interval by the pivot method, rearranging the inequalities correctly.
Write the two-sided interval and both one-sided bounds for a normal mean, with σ known and unknown.
Build an interval for a normal variance using the chi-square pivot, and explain its asymmetry.
Answer the width questions: the dependence on n, the sample size to halve it, and the effect of the confidence level.
State correctly what a confidence level means, and reject the standard misreadings.
traps: An UPPER confidence bound is (−∞, U) and its finite end is ABOVE x̄, so the sign is plus.
A two-sided interval uses the α/2 point; a one-sided bound uses the α point.
The degrees of freedom are n − 1, not n.
Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities, so the LARGER chi-square point gives the LOWER limit for σ².
The variance interval is asymmetric about s²; a symmetric one has been built wrongly.
Width is proportional to 1/√n, so halving it needs four times the data.
The confidence level is a property of the procedure, not a probability about the interval you have.
A confidence interval for μ says nothing about where 95% of the observations lie.

lesson.title: Chi-square Goodness of Fit
objectives: Compute expected frequencies from a claimed distribution and verify that they total n.
Compute the chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic term by term from counts.
Count the degrees of freedom as k − 1 − m across the standard cases, including after pooling.
Apply the upper-tail rejection rule and say why there is no lower critical value.
Check the minimum-expected-count condition, pool adjacent categories when it fails, and recount k.
Say where Yates' correction applies, and read the individual terms to localise a rejection.
traps: The statistic uses FREQUENCIES, never proportions or percentages.
Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ) = 0 always — use it to check your expected counts total n.
The test is upper-tail only; a small statistic is agreement, not evidence.
The minimum-count rule applies to EXPECTED counts, not observed ones.
Pool first, then count k, then subtract — not the other way round.
A normal fit estimates TWO parameters, so df = k − 3.
Yates' correction is for 2 by 2 tables only.
Write the terms one per line; a lost term gives a plausibly wrong answer.

lesson.title: Choosing the Right Test
objectives: Give the five steps of a hypothesis test in order and justify the ordering.
State the p-value correctly and reject the standard misreadings of it.
Say what failing to reject H₀ does and does not establish.
Name the requirements that keep a stated error rate true, including when α and the choice of tail are fixed.
Compute a family-wise error rate, apply the Bonferroni correction, and say why selection by the data cannot be corrected afterwards.
Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance and give the remedy.
Read a situation and name the appropriate test together with the assumption it requires.
traps: The hypothesis comes BEFORE the assumption check — the test determines which assumptions matter.
You cannot compare with tabulated values before computing the statistic.
The p-value is computed assuming H₀, and is not the probability that H₀ is true.
Failing to reject is not accepting; 'accept H₀' is the wrong phrase.
α and the choice of tail are fixed before the data, never after.
The critical region depends on the null distribution and α, not on the observed statistic.
Significance is about consistency with H₀; importance is about magnitude. A large n makes any real effect significant.
Paired data requires the paired test — independence fails, so this is an error and not a preference.
Normality is mild for a test on a mean and critical for a test on a variance.

lesson.title: Contingency Tables: Independence and Homogeneity
objectives: Compute expected counts for a contingency table from its margins and check them against the totals.
Compute the chi-square statistic for a table and count the degrees of freedom as (r − 1)(c − 1).
Derive that rule by counting free cells and by subtracting estimated margins from rc − 1.
Distinguish tests of independence, homogeneity and goodness of fit by the sampling design.
Handle the 2 by 2 case: Yates' correction, the equivalence with the two-proportion z test, and when Fisher's exact test is needed.
Report a measure of association, and say why the statistic alone cannot measure strength.
traps: df = (r − 1)(c − 1), not rc and not rc − 1.
A 3 by 4 and a 4 by 3 table both give 6 — only the product matters.
Expected counts come from the MARGINS: Eᵢⱼ = RᵢCⱼ/n.
Independence and homogeneity differ in design and conclusion, not in arithmetic.
Yates' correction is for 2 by 2 tables only, equivalently for df = 1.
A significant table shows association, never causation.
Doubling every count doubles χ² but leaves the association unchanged.
A 2 by 2 table cannot be pooled, so small expected counts there mean Fisher's exact test.

topics.name: UMP unbiased and UMP invariant tests

lesson.title: UMP Unbiased and UMP Invariant Tests
objectives: Give the argument that no UMP test exists against a two-sided alternative, and identify the disjoint regions it rests on.
Derive both one-sided UMP regions for the exponential rate parameter, with the direction settled correctly.
Show that a one-sided test used against a two-sided alternative is biased, not merely weak.
Define an unbiased test and a UMPU test, and state the two conditions fixing a UMPU test's cut-offs.
Say when the equal-tail test is UMPU, and why the two-sided z test qualifies while the exponential equal-tail test does not.
Define a UMP invariant test, identify the maximal invariant under scale changes, and name the resulting test.
traps: No UMP test exists against a two-sided alternative — that is the answer, not a cleverer region.
In f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx), θ is the RATE, so H₁: θ > θ₀ gives a LOWER tail of Σxᵢ.
The degrees of freedom are 2n, not n.
The lower α point of a chi-square is its upper (1 − α) point.
A one-sided test used two-sided is biased — power below α — not merely low-powered.
The two-tailed region IS a valid size-α test; it just is not UMP.
Equal tails is UMPU only when the null distribution is symmetric.
'Best test' is always relative to a class — name the class.

lesson.title: Order Statistics
objectives: Write the cdf and density of the largest and smallest order statistics for any population.
State the general density of X₍ᵣ₎ and read its constant as a multinomial count.
Show that X₍ᵣ₎ from U(0,1) is Beta(r, n−r+1) and use its mean and variance.
Handle the exponential case, including the minimum's mean θ/n and the maximum's θHₙ.
Compute the expected range and the median's distribution, and use the symmetry shortcut.
State the joint density of all n order statistics and why they are never independent.
traps: The median of n = 5 is X₍₃₎, not X₍₂₎ or the average of two values.
Order statistics are NOT independent — never multiply their marginal densities.
The cdf of the minimum is 1 − [1 − F]ⁿ, not 1 − Fⁿ and not [F]ⁿ.
For U(0,1) the MIDDLE order statistics are the most variable; the pattern reverses for the normal.
The sample median is unbiased for the mean only if the population is symmetric.
E(range) needs only linearity; Var(range) needs the covariance, which is not zero.
E(X₍ₙ₎) for U(0,θ) is nθ/(n+1), so the MLE is biased.
Mind the exponential's parameterisation: pdf e^(−x) has mean 1; (1/θ)e^(−x/θ) has mean θ.

lesson.title: Conditional Distributions
objectives: Derive conditional pmfs and densities from joint and marginal distributions.
Determine conditional support from the joint support.
Recognise independence through conditional and marginal laws.
Compute conditional expectations and variances.
Use the conditional bivariate normal distribution.
traps: Use the marginal of the variable being conditioned on.
Write the conditional support before dividing.
A conditional density must integrate to one on its support.
f(X|Y) and f(Y|X) are directional and generally differ.
For a bivariate normal pair, conditional variance is independent of y.
Independence requires conditional law to equal marginal law almost everywhere.

lesson.title: Conditional Expectation, Total Variance and Mixtures
objectives: Say what E(Y | X) is and why it has a mean and a variance of its own.
State and apply the tower property and the law of total variance.
Derive the law of total variance from Var(Y) = E(Y²) − [E(Y)]².
Compute both terms in two-stage models, including when the conditional variance depends on X.
Show that any Poisson mixture is overdispersed and compute its variance.
Name the Poisson–Gamma, Binomial–Beta and Normal–Normal mixtures and their marginals.
traps: E(Y | X) is a random variable, not a number.
Var(Y) is NOT E[Var(Y|X)] — the between term is missing.
For a mixed Poisson, Var(Y) = E(X) + Var(X) always exceeds the mean.
Y | X ~ N(X, 1) with X ~ N(0, σ²) gives Var(Y) = 1 + σ², not σ².
When Var(Y|X) depends on X, the within term needs E(X²), not [E(X)]².
Mind the exponential's parameterisation: mean 1/λ means variance 1/λ².
1/λ + 1/λ² = (λ + 1)/λ², not λ(λ + 1)/λ².
Independence makes the between term zero, not the within term.

lesson.title: MGFs, Cumulants and Central Moments
objectives: Define an MGF and identify its interval of existence around zero.
Obtain raw moments by differentiating the MGF at zero.
Use products and substitutions for independent sums and affine transformations.
Derive cumulants from the log-MGF and use additivity.
Convert raw moments, central moments and cumulants correctly.
traps: M''(0) is E(X²), not Var(X).
An MGF must exist near zero for the usual uniqueness result.
Independent MGFs multiply; cumulant functions add.
κ₄=μ₄−3σ⁴, not μ₄.
For aX+b, κ_r=aʳκ_r(X) for r≥2; translation changes only κ₁.
The lognormal has no finite MGF for positive t.

lesson.title: Standard Discrete Distributions
objectives: Identify a discrete family from what is fixed and what is counted.
State the pmf, mean, variance and mgf of the binomial, Poisson, geometric and negative binomial.
Use the variance-to-mean ratio as an independent check on an identification.
Explain why the geometric has no fixed dispersion direction, with p = 0.5 as the boundary.
State the limits and closures: negative binomial at r = 1, binomial to Poisson, Poisson additivity.
Say why sampling without replacement gives a hypergeometric and what the correction factor does.
traps: 'A finite number of trials' means binomial; 'the rᵗʰ success' means negative binomial. Read which is fixed.
The geometric's variance does NOT always exceed its mean — the ratio is q/p, equal at p = 0.5.
Poisson rates ADD: Poisson(2) + Poisson(3) is Poisson(5), not Poisson(6).
Sampling without replacement is hypergeometric, not binomial — the means agree, the variances do not.
Mind the geometric convention: counting trials gives mean 1/p, counting failures gives q/p.
A binomial's variance is always below its mean, so a binomial can never be equidispersed.
The negative binomial's ratio 1/p does not involve r, so r never affects whether it is overdispersed.
A variance-to-mean ratio of 1 narrows the field but does not prove the Poisson — a geometric with p = 0.5 has it too.

lesson.title: Standard Continuous Distributions
objectives: Identify support and parameterisation of the main continuous distribution families.
Compute probabilities from PDFs, CDFs and survival functions.
Distinguish exponential and gamma rate from scale conventions.
Calculate means and variances for uniform, exponential, gamma, beta and normal laws.
Recognise chi-square, t and F distributions and their parameter roles.
traps: Identify support before choosing a family.
For exponential rate λ, mean=1/λ; for scale θ, mean=θ.
Gamma rate and scale are reciprocals.
Beta is supported on (0,1); Gamma and chi-square on (0,∞).
For continuous X, P(X=x)=0 even if f(x)>0.
F degrees of freedom are ordered: numerator first, denominator second.

lesson.title: Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev and Cauchy–Schwarz
objectives: Decide convexity by the second derivative and get Jensen's direction right.
Rule on the June 2026 four-statement question and say why E(1/X) ≤ 1/E(X) is false.
Apply Markov and Chebyshev, naming the assumption each requires.
Construct the distributions that attain each bound and verify them.
Use the tail identities for E(X) and E(X²) and the discrete sum for a waiting time.
Derive |ρ| ≤ 1 from Cauchy–Schwarz and state the equality condition.
traps: E(1/X) ≥ 1/E(X), NOT ≤ — 1/x is convex. This is the exam's trap.
Jensen REVERSES for a concave function; log x and √x go the other way from x² and 1/x.
Markov requires X ≥ 0. Without it the statement is false.
Chebyshev at k = 1 gives the bound 1, which is no information at all.
Do not halve the two-sided Chebyshev bound for a one-sided tail; use Cantelli's 1/(1 + k²).
E(1/X) can be INFINITE — for Exponential(1) it diverges, so simulations misbehave.
The bounds are for proving things, not for computing probabilities you could compute exactly.
A sample mean that drifts upward with n signals a non-existent expectation, not a coding bug.

lesson.title: Independence and Inclusion–Exclusion
objectives: Turn 'at least one' into 1 − ∏P(Aᵢᶜ) and say where independence is used.
Compute complements explicitly, and handle exponents that add to n(n+1)/2.
Distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity, including the null-event exception.
Give a counterexample showing pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.
State Bonferroni's inequality, note it needs no assumptions, and say when it is tight.
Apply inclusion–exclusion for two and three events and explain why it is impractical beyond that.
traps: In Q34 the exponent is n(n+1)/2, not n — multiplying 1/2ⁱ adds the exponents.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are DEPENDENT, not independent.
ΣP(Aᵢ) is an expected count and a Bonferroni bound, not a union probability — it can exceed 1.
Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.
P(Aᵢ) = 1 − 1/2ⁱ and P(Aᵢ) = 1/2ⁱ give completely different answers: 0.0000305 against 0.298 at n = 5.
The complement route needs independence; without it the answer can be wrong in either direction.
A null event IS independent of everything, so the exclusivity rule needs both probabilities positive.
n(n+1)/2 is the sum 1 + ⋯ + n; n(n−1)/2 counts pairs.

lesson.title: Convergence, WLLN, SLLN and CLT
objectives: Distinguish almost-sure, in-probability and distributional convergence.
State weak and strong laws with their assumptions.
Use Chebyshev's inequality to establish convergence in probability.
Apply the central limit theorem to sample means and sums.
Interpret the CLT as an asymptotic law for scaled errors, not an exact finite-sample identity.
traps: Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, but not conversely in general.
WLLN concerns convergence in probability; SLLN concerns almost-sure convergence.
CLT concerns the scaled error, not the unscaled sample mean.
Use σ/√n as the standard error, not σ²/n.
The finite-variance CLT is asymptotic, not an exact finite-sample normal law.
Chebyshev gives an upper bound; it is not a normal approximation.

lesson.title: Transformations and Jacobians
objectives: Choose between the cdf route, the Jacobian route and the conditional-ratio route.
Compute a Jacobian determinant and say why the density is multiplied by it.
Derive that X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s) and explain where the rate cancels.
Give the sum as Gamma(n, λ) and the minimum as exponential(nλ) without confusing them.
Condition Poisson counts on a total to get a binomial, and binomials to get a hypergeometric.
Apply memorylessness correctly, including the exponent.
traps: X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s), NOT Gamma(2, λ) — the Gamma is the distribution of the SUM.
The sum of n exponentials is Gamma(n, λ); the MINIMUM is exponential(nλ). Do not swap them.
The minimum has rate nλ, not λ/n — it arrives sooner, not later.
E(X | X + Y = s) = s/2, not 1/λ; the conditional answer must contain s and not λ.
Two binomials given their total give a HYPERGEOMETRIC, not a binomial.
In P(T > 6 | T > 4) with rate 2, the exponent is 2 × 2 = 4, not 2 or 6.
The Jacobian formula needs the map to be one-to-one; Y = X² needs both branches.
A conditional-given-the-total answer containing the rate has failed to cancel something.

lesson.title: Characteristic Functions
objectives: Define the characteristic function and explain why it always exists.
Compute CFs for Bernoulli, Poisson, normal and uniform laws.
Use independence, scaling and translation identities.
Recover moments from derivatives when the moments exist.
Apply uniqueness and Lévy continuity to identify distributions and limits.
traps: A CF always exists; an MGF may fail to exist near zero.
φ(0)=1 and |φ(t)|≤1 are necessary properties.
Independent sums multiply CFs; dependence prevents automatic factorisation.
For aX+b, φ(t)=e^{itb}φ_X(at).
φ'(0)=iE(X), not E(X) directly.
Equal CFs imply equal distributions; equal moments alone need not.

lesson.title: Bayes Theorem and Conditional Probability
objectives: Compute conditional probabilities using the multiplication rule.
Use partitions and the law of total probability.
Apply Bayes theorem to reverse conditional probabilities.
Interpret prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV.
Recognise independence and avoid base-rate neglect in diagnostic problems.
traps: P(A|B) and P(B|A) are not interchangeable.
The total-probability denominator must include every partition cell.
False-positive rate is 1−specificity, not specificity.
PPV depends on prevalence; sensitivity alone does not determine it.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are not independent.
Use P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B) consistently.

topics.name: Sampling distributions: t, chi-square and F

lesson.title: Sampling Distributions: t, Chi-square, F and the Correlation Coefficient
objectives: Build chi-square, t and F from sums of squares of normals and use the identity t² = F(1, k).
Write the exact null density of r and read its shape from the exponent (n − 4)/2.
Derive the n = 3 arcsine and n = 4 uniform results from one symmetric Beta.
Run the exact t test of ρ = 0 and convert it into a critical value for |r|.
Explain the skew of r as ρ → 1 and its degeneracy at ρ = ±1.
Build and interpret a Fisher-z confidence interval for ρ, including its asymmetry.
traps: The distribution of r is NOT non-degenerate for every population — at ρ = ±1 it collapses to a point.
As ρ → 1 the distribution of r becomes more skewed, not more normal.
Fisher's z has variance 1/(n − 3), not 1/(n − 1) or 1/n.
The exact t test covers only ρ = 0; it cannot test ρ = ρ₀ ≠ 0 or give an interval.
The degrees of freedom are n − 2, not n − 1: a mean was fitted for each variable.
A confidence interval for ρ is NOT symmetric about r; back-transform each endpoint with tanh.
r = 0 means no linear association, not independence.
At n = 4 the 5% critical |r| is 0.95 — a large r from a tiny sample is not evidence.

topics.name: Hat matrix, residual maker, quadratic forms

lesson.title: 6.1 — Hat Matrix, Residual Maker and Quadratic Forms
objectives: Derive the hat matrix H and residual-maker matrix M from the OLS projection.
Prove that H and M are symmetric and idempotent under full-column-rank OLS.
Use H and M to express fitted values, residuals, SSE and residual orthogonality.
Connect trace and rank of projection matrices to model and residual degrees of freedom.
Evaluate quadratic forms involving symmetric idempotent matrices.
Avoid confusing the hat matrix, residual maker, projection space and their ranks.
traps: H projects y onto C(X), while M projects y onto the orthogonal complement of C(X).
H and M are both symmetric and idempotent; M=I−H.
rank(H)=trace(H)=k when X has full column rank k; rank(M)=trace(M)=n−k.
H is n×n, not k×k.
The diagonal entries hᵢᵢ are leverage values; they are not generally all equal.
The residual vector is e=My and satisfies X′e=0.
For a symmetric idempotent matrix A, y′Ay is nonnegative and has rank(A) degrees of freedom under a standard normal vector.

lesson.title: 6.2 — Gauss–Markov, BLUE and Estimability
objectives: State the Gauss–Markov assumptions and conclusion without adding a normality assumption.
Derive the OLS estimator and its variance–covariance matrix.
Explain why OLS is BLUE among linear unbiased estimators.
Determine whether a linear function of regression parameters is estimable using the row space of the design matrix.
Solve the June 2026 BLUE question and verify every coefficient and divisor.
traps: BLUE means best (minimum variance) among linear unbiased estimators, not among all estimators.
Normality is not required for the Gauss–Markov theorem.
Under V(u)=σ²I, Var(β̂)=σ²(X′X)⁻¹ when X has full column rank.
For rank-deficient X, do not blindly invert X′X; only estimable functions have unique unbiased linear estimators.
A′β is estimable iff a lies in the row space of X (equivalently a is in C(X′)).
The June 2026 question's divisors are 6 for β̂₁ and 2 for β̂₂.

topics.name: ANOVA decomposition and the F test from R²

lesson.title: 6.3 — ANOVA Decomposition and the Overall F Test
objectives: Derive the corrected-total sum-of-squares decomposition for regression with an intercept.
Construct the regression ANOVA table and identify degrees of freedom and mean squares.
Derive the overall F statistic for testing all slope coefficients jointly.
Express the overall F statistic in terms of R², n and k.
Distinguish the overall F test from individual t tests and partial F tests.
Interpret numerator and denominator degrees of freedom correctly.
traps: Use k as the total number of estimated parameters including the intercept; the number of tested slopes is k−1.
For the overall regression test, numerator df=k−1 and denominator df=n−k.
F=[R²/(k−1)]/[(1−R²)/(n−k)], not a product.
The overall F test tests all slope coefficients jointly; it is not the same as testing one coefficient with a t statistic.
In simple linear regression with one slope, overall F equals the square of the slope t statistic.
Corrected TSS=RegSS+RSS for OLS with an intercept.
Adding a predictor cannot increase RSS in nested OLS and cannot decrease R²; adjusted R² may move either way.
A large F is evidence against the joint null, not proof of causality or correct specification.

lesson.title: 6.4 — R², Adjusted R² and Model Comparison
objectives: Define R² through regression, residual and total sums of squares.
Explain why ordinary R² cannot decrease when a predictor is added to a nested OLS model with an intercept.
Derive and calculate adjusted R² using consistent parameter-count conventions.
Interpret negative adjusted R² and distinguish it from ordinary R².
Compare models while accounting for sample size and number of estimated parameters.
Recognize limitations of R² and adjusted R² as model-selection criteria.
traps: R²=1−RSS/TSS=RegSS/TSS for ordinary least squares with an intercept.
Adding predictors to a nested OLS model cannot reduce ordinary R²; it can stay the same or increase.
Adjusted R² can decrease when a predictor is added because it penalizes model size.
Adjusted R² can be negative; ordinary R² with an intercept and the usual in-sample definition lies between 0 and 1.
Do not compare adjusted R² across models fitted to different response variables or different samples without careful justification.
A high R² does not prove causality, correct specification, or good out-of-sample prediction.
For k counting all parameters including the intercept, adjusted R²=1−[(RSS/(n−k))/(TSS/(n−1))].
For a model with p predictors excluding the intercept, k=p+1 and residual df=n−p−1.

lesson.title: 6.5 — Multicollinearity
objectives: Distinguish perfect from near multicollinearity using the rank and conditioning of the design matrix.
Explain why multicollinearity inflates sampling variances and standard errors of affected coefficient estimates.
Identify what multicollinearity does not automatically cause: OLS bias or loss of overall fit.
Interpret high R² with weak individual t-statistics and unstable coefficient estimates.
Evaluate remedies and distinguish prediction goals from coefficient-interpretation goals.
Answer the June 2026 Paper 2 Q38 negation question and its linked variants.
traps: Multicollinearity does not, by itself, bias OLS when the exogeneity assumption holds.
Near multicollinearity increases variances/standard errors; it does not necessarily make coefficient estimates large in magnitude.
Perfect multicollinearity makes X′X singular, so unique separate OLS coefficients cannot be computed by the ordinary inverse formula.
A high R² with individually insignificant t-statistics can be a symptom, not a proof, of multicollinearity.
Multicollinearity does not automatically destroy prediction within the observed predictor range.
Dropping a relevant predictor can introduce omitted-variable bias; it is not a harmless universal remedy.
The June 2026 Q38 asks what is NOT a consequence: bias is the correct answer (C).

lesson.title: 6.6 — Heteroscedasticity and Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
objectives: Define heteroscedasticity through the conditional error variance.
Distinguish unbiasedness of OLS coefficients from efficiency and validity of conventional standard errors.
Recognize the limits of residual plots and formal heteroscedasticity tests.
Derive the weighted least squares transformation for known unequal variances.
Explain feasible GLS when the variance structure is estimated.
Choose robust standard errors or WLS/FGLS according to the inferential or modelling objective.
traps: Heteroscedasticity means Var(uᵢ|X)=σᵢ² is not constant across observations; it does not mean the conditional mean is nonzero.
Under exogeneity and a correctly specified conditional mean, OLS can remain unbiased/consistent despite heteroscedasticity.
Conventional homoscedastic OLS standard errors are generally incorrect; the direction of error is not universally upward.
OLS is generally inefficient among linear unbiased estimators when the covariance matrix is non-spherical.
White/heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors change estimated uncertainty, not the OLS coefficient estimates.
If Ω is known and positive definite, GLS uses Ω⁻¹; WLS is the diagonal special case.
For Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²hᵢ, WLS weights are proportional to 1/hᵢ, not 1/σᵢ.
FGLS substitutes an estimated covariance structure and therefore adds estimation uncertainty; it is not automatically superior in small samples.
Breusch–Pagan tests a specified variance relation; White's test is more general but can consume degrees of freedom.
Do not confuse heteroscedasticity with autocorrelation: one concerns unequal variances, the other cross-observation covariance.

lesson.title: 6.7 — Autocorrelation and the Durbin–Watson Test
objectives: Define autocorrelation in regression disturbances and distinguish it from heteroscedasticity.
Explain how serial correlation affects OLS efficiency and conventional standard errors.
Recognize positive and negative serial correlation from residual patterns.
Calculate and interpret the Durbin–Watson statistic.
State the hypotheses, bounds and limitations of the Durbin–Watson test.
Identify when alternative tests or GLS-type corrections are needed.
traps: Autocorrelation is covariance across different observations; heteroscedasticity is non-constant variance within observations.
With exogeneity, serial correlation alone need not bias OLS coefficients, but OLS is generally inefficient and conventional standard errors are unreliable.
DW is approximately 2(1−r̂₁), where r̂₁ is the first-order sample residual autocorrelation.
DW values near 0 suggest positive first-order serial correlation; values near 2 suggest none; values near 4 suggest negative serial correlation.
The DW statistic lies between 0 and 4.
The usual DW bounds test has an inconclusive region; do not force a decision when d lies between dL and dU (or their upper-tail counterparts).
The standard DW test is not appropriate in its usual form when lagged dependent variables are included among regressors.
DW tests first-order serial correlation, not every possible higher-order dependence pattern.
Durbin's h or Breusch–Godfrey LM may be needed in dynamic models or for higher-order serial correlation.
Do not confuse a DW statistic with a p-value; formal decisions use bounds or an appropriate reference procedure.

lesson.title: 6.8 — Endogeneity and Instrumental Variables
objectives: Explain why correlation between a regressor and the disturbance invalidates the usual OLS argument.
Distinguish exogeneity, relevance and exclusion in an instrumental-variable design.
Derive the just-identified IV estimator as a ratio of reduced-form and first-stage effects.
Interpret the direction of OLS bias in a simple omitted-confounder or simultaneity setting.
Recognise weak-instrument symptoms and distinguish them from invalid instruments.
Choose an IV design and state the assumptions that make its causal interpretation credible.
traps: A regressor is endogenous when it is correlated with the structural disturbance; this is not the same as saying the regressor is random.
OLS exogeneity is E(u|X)=0 in the conditional formulation; zero unconditional mean E(u)=0 alone is not enough.
Instrument relevance requires a nonzero relationship with the endogenous regressor, conditional on included exogenous controls.
Instrument exclusion requires that the instrument affect the outcome only through the endogenous regressor; relevance does not establish exclusion.
The just-identified IV estimator is the reduced-form effect divided by the first-stage effect.
A weak instrument can make IV estimates noisy and conventional large-sample approximations unreliable; it is not the same as an invalid instrument.
Overidentification tests assess joint restrictions under maintained assumptions; they do not prove every instrument is valid.
Adding controls does not automatically remove endogeneity if unobserved confounding, simultaneity or measurement error remains.

lesson.title: 6.9 — Identification in Simultaneous Equation Models
objectives: Distinguish structural equations from reduced-form equations in a simultaneous system.
Identify endogenous and predetermined or exogenous variables in a structural model.
Explain why OLS applied directly to a structural equation is generally inconsistent when endogenous regressors appear on its right-hand side.
Apply the order condition to classify an equation as underidentified, exactly identified or overidentified.
Apply the rank condition and explain why it is necessary and sufficient while the order condition is only necessary.
Interpret excluded exogenous variables as sources of identifying variation.
traps: Structural coefficients describe behavioural equations; reduced-form coefficients describe equilibrium responses to exogenous variables.
An endogenous variable is jointly determined inside the system; an exogenous variable is determined outside the system.
The order condition counts excluded exogenous variables and endogenous right-hand-side variables, not all regressors.
The order condition is necessary but not sufficient; a zero cross-equation coefficient can still make the rank condition fail.
Exactly identified means the number of excluded exogenous variables equals the number of endogenous RHS variables and the rank condition holds.
Overidentified means there are more excluded exogenous variables than endogenous RHS variables; the rank condition must still hold.
A variable's exclusion from one equation is a modelling restriction, not proof that it is irrelevant in the full system.
The reduced form does not generally identify every structural coefficient without additional restrictions.

lesson.title: 6.10 — Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
objectives: Explain why 2SLS is used when structural regressors are endogenous.
Construct the instrument matrix from included exogenous regressors and excluded instruments.
Estimate the first-stage regression and interpret fitted endogenous regressors.
Describe the second stage and distinguish it from a naive two-step standard-error calculation.
Write the matrix 2SLS estimator using the projection matrix P_Z.
Recognise identification, weak-instrument and overidentification issues in a 2SLS design.
traps: The instrument matrix contains all exogenous regressors, including included exogenous controls and excluded instruments.
The first stage regresses each endogenous RHS variable on the full instrument set.
The second stage regresses Y on included exogenous controls and fitted endogenous regressors.
Fitted values are generated by projecting endogenous regressors onto the instrument space.
The matrix estimator is (X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY, with P_Z=Z(Z′Z)⁻¹Z′ when Z has full column rank.
A naive OLS standard error from treating fitted values as observed regressors is generally wrong; use the 2SLS covariance estimator.
With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument, 2SLS equals the just-identified IV/Wald ratio.
2SLS does not cure invalid instruments or weak relevance.

lesson.title: 6.11 — Dummy Variables and Qualitative Regressors
objectives: Represent qualitative categories using indicator variables in a regression model.
Choose and interpret a reference category and avoid the dummy-variable trap.
Determine the number of dummy variables needed for a categorical predictor.
Interpret intercept shifts and slope changes using interaction terms.
Use seasonal or group indicators correctly in regression models.
Interpret dummy coefficients in level-log and log-level settings with appropriate care.
traps: With an intercept and k mutually exclusive categories, include k−1 dummy variables.
The omitted category is the reference group; its effect is absorbed into the intercept.
Including all k category dummies with an intercept creates exact linear dependence.
A dummy coefficient without an interaction is an intercept difference, holding other regressors fixed.
A dummy-by-continuous-variable interaction allows the slope to differ across groups.
The group-specific slope is the base slope plus the interaction coefficient.
For monthly seasonal indicators with an intercept, use 11 dummies and choose one reference month.
In a log-linear model, 100β is an approximation; the exact percentage difference is 100(exp(β)−1).

lesson.title: 6.12 — Logistic Regression for Binary Responses
objectives: Explain why the linear probability model can produce probabilities outside the unit interval and heteroscedastic errors.
Write the logistic regression model using the logit link and convert a linear predictor into a probability.
Interpret logistic coefficients as changes in log-odds and exponentiated coefficients as odds ratios.
Calculate fitted probabilities and marginal effects at specified covariate values.
Describe maximum-likelihood estimation, likelihood-ratio tests and deviance.
Recognise complete separation, classification thresholds and the distinction between probability and odds.
traps: The logistic model is linear in the log-odds, not in the probability.
The fitted probability is exp(η)/(1+exp(η)), which always lies strictly between zero and one for finite η.
A coefficient β_j changes log-odds per unit x_j; exp(β_j) is the multiplicative change in odds.
An odds ratio is not a probability ratio or a percentage-point change in probability.
The marginal effect in a simple logit model is βp(1−p), so it depends on the covariate values through p.
Logistic coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, not ordinary least squares.
Deviance is based on log-likelihood; a smaller deviance indicates better fit relative to the saturated model.
Complete separation can make ordinary maximum-likelihood estimates diverge.

topics.name: Restricted regression: exact, stochastic and mixed restrictions

lesson.title: 6.13 — Restricted Regression and Linear Hypothesis Testing
objectives: Express restrictions on regression coefficients in the matrix form Rβ=r.
Distinguish unrestricted OLS from restricted least squares.
Calculate a restricted least-squares estimate for a simple linear restriction.
Use the extra sum-of-squares F statistic to test q linear restrictions.
Recognise the equivalence F=t² for a single linear restriction.
Distinguish exact restrictions from stochastic restrictions and explain mixed estimation.
traps: A linear restriction has the form Rβ=r, where R has q independent rows.
Restricted least squares minimises RSS subject to the restrictions; its RSS cannot be smaller than unrestricted OLS RSS.
The extra sum-of-squares F statistic is [(RSS_R−RSS_U)/q]/[RSS_U/(n−k)] for q restrictions.
The unrestricted model is nested within the restricted model in the sense that the restriction defines a subset of the parameter space.
For one restriction, the classical F statistic equals the square of the corresponding t statistic.
Exact restrictions impose a fixed equality; stochastic restrictions allow deviations with a specified variance.
Mixed estimation combines sample information with external or prior linear information.
A restriction matrix with redundant rows does not represent q independent restrictions; use its rank.

topics.name: Errors in variables and stochastic regressors

lesson.title: 6.14 — Errors in Variables and Measurement Error
objectives: Distinguish classical measurement error in a regressor from measurement error in the response.
Derive the attenuation factor in a simple regression with classical regressor measurement error.
Interpret the reliability ratio and calculate the attenuated probability limit.
Distinguish classical measurement error from Berkson measurement error.
Explain how a valid instrument can address measurement error in an endogenous regressor.
Recognise why multivariate measurement error can affect several coefficients and not merely attenuate one slope.
traps: Classical regressor measurement error is W=X+v, where v is mean-zero and independent of X and u.
In a simple regression, classical measurement error in X attenuates the slope toward zero under the standard assumptions.
The reliability ratio is λ=Var(X)/[Var(X)+Var(v)], between zero and one.
The probability limit of the naive slope is λβ, not β, under the classical single-regressor setup.
Independent mean-zero measurement error in Y increases residual variance but does not bias the slope under standard assumptions.
Berkson error is often represented as X=W+v, the reverse conditioning structure from classical error W=X+v.
An IV correction requires an instrument correlated with the true regressor but uncorrelated with the measurement error and structural disturbance.
With multiple regressors, measurement error can bias several coefficients in directions that are not all simple attenuation.

lesson.title: 6.15 — k-Class Estimators, LIML and Fuller Estimation
objectives: Write the general k-class estimator using the instrument residual-maker matrix.
Show that the k-class estimator reduces to OLS at κ=0 and 2SLS at κ=1.
Interpret the role of the projection and residual-maker matrices in the estimator.
Calculate a simple scalar k-class estimate for specified cross-products.
Explain how LIML chooses its k-class parameter and how Fuller modifies LIML.
Compare OLS, 2SLS and LIML while recognising that no estimator repairs invalid instruments.
traps: The k-class parameter κ is not the number of regressors or restrictions.
M_Z=I−P_Z is the residual-maker matrix for projection onto the instrument space.
The general estimator is [X′(I−κM_Z)X]⁻¹X′(I−κM_Z)Y.
At κ=0, I−κM_Z=I and the estimator is OLS.
At κ=1, I−M_Z=P_Z and the estimator is 2SLS.
LIML selects κ from the likelihood/eigenvalue formulation; it is a member of the k-class family.
Fuller estimation applies a finite-sample adjustment to LIML.
LIML can have favourable finite-sample bias properties with many or weak instruments, but it does not eliminate weak-identification or invalid-instrument problems.

lesson.title: Markov Chains: n-step Probabilities and Chapman–Kolmogorov
objectives: Define a discrete-time Markov chain and state the Markov property in words and symbols.
Construct and check a transition matrix using the row-stochastic convention used here.
Compute two-step and n-step transition probabilities using matrix powers.
Apply the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation by conditioning on an intermediate state.
traps: The convention here uses rows as current states and columns as next states; each row sums to one.
P² is not obtained by squaring each entry; it is ordinary matrix multiplication.
For a two-step transition, multiply along each possible intermediate state and add the path probabilities.
The Markov property says the present state screens off the past; it does not say successive states are independent.
A stationary distribution is not automatically the limiting distribution; periodicity and reducibility matter.

lesson.title: Stationary Distributions: Solving πP = π
objectives: Define a stationary distribution and verify it by multiplication.
Find stationary probabilities by solving πP=π together with the sum-to-one condition.
Solve two-state and three-state transition-matrix problems exactly.
Distinguish existence, uniqueness and convergence to a stationary distribution.
traps: With row distributions, use πP=π. A column-vector convention changes the equation.
Do not use every equation in πP=π as independent; one is redundant for a stochastic matrix.
Always impose πᵢ≥0 and Σᵢπᵢ=1. An eigenvector alone need not be a probability vector.
Existence does not imply uniqueness. A reducible chain can have many stationary distributions.
Uniqueness does not by itself guarantee convergence from every starting state; periodicity can prevent convergence.
A stationary distribution describes an invariant distribution, not necessarily the observed long-run fraction of time without further conditions.

topics.name: First passage and first return, mean passage time

lesson.title: First Passage and First Return Times
objectives: Define the relevant Markov-chain quantity and interpret it correctly.
Set up equations using the transition matrix and the correct boundary conditions.
Solve finite-state examples exactly and verify the result.
Recognise assumptions, limiting cases and common UGC NET examination traps.
traps: Do not confuse first passage with occupancy at a fixed time.
Do not forget that the target has zero remaining hitting time.
A hitting probability must lie in [0,1]; a mean time need not be an integer.
Communication is mutual reachability; a one-way path is insufficient.
A closed class has no outgoing transition.
Period is a gcd, not the smallest return time.

lesson.title: Classification of States: Communication, Recurrence and Periodicity
objectives: Determine whether two states communicate using directed reachability.
Identify communicating classes and test whether each class is closed.
Classify states as transient or recurrent in a finite chain.
Calculate the period from the set of possible positive return times.
traps: Do not confuse first passage with occupancy at a fixed time.
Do not forget that the target has zero remaining hitting time.
A hitting probability must lie in [0,1]; a mean time need not be an integer.
Communication is mutual reachability; a one-way path is insufficient.
A closed class has no outgoing transition.
Period is a gcd, not the smallest return time.

lesson.title: Poisson Process: Counts, Inter-arrival Times and Waiting Times
objectives: Recognise the defining assumptions and rate parameter of a homogeneous Poisson process.
Calculate event-count probabilities using N(t) ~ Poisson(λt).
Derive and use exponential inter-arrival and waiting-time distributions.
Find the distribution and moments of the time to the kth event.
Use independent and stationary increments and the exponential memoryless property without confusing counts with waiting times.
traps: λ is a rate per unit time; λt is the expected count over an interval of length t.
Use the same time unit for λ and t.
P(N(t)=n) is a count probability; P(T₁>t) is a waiting-time survival probability.
The inter-arrival time is exponential with mean 1/λ, not λ.
The time to the kth event is Gamma/Erlang, not exponential when k>1.
Independent increments apply to disjoint intervals; stationary increments depend only on interval length.
At an arbitrary time, the residual waiting time is exponential by memorylessness; this is not a claim that all conditional waiting questions are identical.

lesson.title: Simple Random Walk and Gambler’s Ruin
objectives: Define a simple random walk and identify its drift from step probabilities.
Calculate the position distribution after n steps using the number of upward steps.
Set up and solve gambler’s ruin probabilities using first-step recurrence and boundary conditions.
Find expected duration until absorption in the fair and biased cases.
Interpret the fair-game and biased-game results and recognise common boundary and indexing errors.
traps: Define the state as the current fortune before writing the recurrence.
At an interior state i, p_i = p p_{i+1}+q p_{i−1}; do not reverse p and q.
Use boundary values u_0=0 and u_N=1 when asking for the probability of reaching N before 0.
For a fair walk, the ruin probability from i is 1−i/N; the probability of reaching N first is i/N.
For a biased walk, the ratio q/p determines the powers in the solution.
The expected absorption time for a fair walk is i(N−i), in step units.
Do not confuse eventual ruin probability with expected time to ruin or absorption.

lesson.title: Birth–Death Processes and M/M/1 Queues
objectives: Represent a birth–death process using state-dependent birth and death rates.
Write the forward balance equations and identify stationary probabilities.
Derive the stationary distribution of an M/M/1 queue and its stability condition.
Calculate utilisation, idle probability, mean queue length, mean system size and waiting times.
Distinguish customers in the queue from customers in the whole system and apply Little’s law.
traps: Birth and death rates depend on the current state; do not assume constant rates unless specified.
For M/M/1, λ is the arrival rate and μ is the service rate.
A stationary distribution exists only when λ<μ; ρ=λ/μ must be below one.
P(N=n)=(1−ρ)ρⁿ includes n=0; the queue is empty with probability 1−ρ.
L is the mean number in the whole system; Lq excludes the customer in service.
W is time in the whole system; Wq is waiting time before service.
Use the same time unit for λ and μ.

lesson.title: Branching Processes and Extinction Probability
objectives: Define a Galton–Watson branching process and state its independence assumptions.
Construct the offspring probability-generating function and obtain its mean.
Derive the recursion for extinction by generation n.
Find the eventual extinction probability as the smallest solution of f(s)=s in [0,1].
Classify extinction behaviour using the offspring mean and check boundary cases.
traps: The offspring count is per individual in one generation, not the total population.
Offspring counts of different individuals and generations are independent and identically distributed in the classical Galton–Watson model.
The extinction probability is the smallest root of f(s)=s in [0,1], not any root selected arbitrarily.
If m>1, extinction is not automatically impossible; it can still have positive probability.
The statement m≤1 implies certain extinction needs the non-degenerate qualification; if every individual has exactly one child, extinction never occurs.
Extinction by generation n and eventual extinction are different events.
The mean population E[Z_n]=m^n does not determine the probability of extinction by itself.

lesson.title: Renewal Processes and Long-Run Reward
objectives: Define a renewal process from iid positive inter-renewal times.
Construct renewal epochs and the counting process N(t).
Distinguish inter-arrival time, renewal count and renewal function.
Use the renewal equation and elementary renewal theorem in elementary cases.
Apply the renewal-reward theorem.
traps: Renewal epochs are cumulative sums, not individual gaps.
N(t) counts renewals by t; m(t)=E[N(t)] is the renewal function.
The long-run renewal rate is 1/μ, not μ.
The elementary renewal theorem is asymptotic, not an exact finite-time formula.
The renewal-reward rate is E[R]/E[X].

lesson.title: Stationarity and Invertibility
objectives: State stationarity and invertibility as root conditions on two polynomials.
Apply the AR(2) stationarity triangle and give its three vertices.
Classify order-1 and order-2 processes into the four categories.
Explain why a finite MA is always stationary and a pure AR always invertible.
Expand a stationary AR(1) as an infinite MA and an invertible MA(1) as an infinite AR.
Say why θ and 1/θ are observationally identical and what invertibility achieves.
traps: φ₁ > 1 does NOT rule out stationarity: (1.2, −0.4) is stationary.
All THREE inequalities must hold; checking one or two is not enough.
(1.2, −0.2) sums to exactly 1 and has a unit root — a boundary case, not a stationary one.
A finite MA is always stationary; only invertibility can fail.
A pure AR is always invertible; there is no MA polynomial to constrain.
The invertibility region in θ is the SAME triangle as the stationarity region in φ.
θ and 1/θ give identical autocorrelations, so |θ| > 1 is never reported.
On a boundary, trust algebra over a numerical root-finder: 1.0 can compute as 1.0000000000000002.

lesson.title: ACF and PACF Identification
objectives: State the identification rule for AR, MA and ARMA and say which function cuts off.
Explain the cut-off for an MA from disjoint shock windows and for an AR from the regression interpretation.
Apply the ±2/√n bands pointwise and ignore isolated excursions.
Recover φ from an AR(1) ACF and the invertible θ from an MA(1) lag-1 autocorrelation.
Use φₚₚ = φₚ to read the last autoregressive coefficient from the PACF.
Use the bound |ρ₁| ≤ 0.5 to rule out an MA(1), and recognise a non-stationary ACF.
traps: The letters are CROSSED: the ACF reads MA order, the PACF reads AR order.
An alternating ACF means a negative coefficient, not an MA component.
|ρ₁| ≤ 0.5 for ANY MA(1) — a larger value rules the model out.
The bands are pointwise, so one or two excursions over twenty lags are expected.
An isolated spike at an uninterpretable lag is noise; a spike at the seasonal period is not.
An ACF decaying almost linearly means non-stationarity, not a high-order AR.
Both functions decaying is the ARMA diagnostic, not a failed reading.
Identification comes AFTER the stationarity check, never before it.

lesson.title: The Yule–Walker Equations
objectives: Derive the Yule–Walker equations and say why the shock term vanishes for k ≥ 1.
Solve the AR(2) system in closed form and estimate the coefficients from a sample ACF.
Predict the sign of φ₂ from ρ₂ against ρ₁², and recognise r₂ = r₁² as an AR(1) signature.
State the AR(1) and AR(2) stationarity conditions and apply the AR(2) triangle.
Recognise a unit root from φ₁ + φ₂ = 1, factor out the difference operator, and find the ACF of the differenced series.
Identify an AR or MA order from the cut-off pattern of the ACF and PACF.
traps: ρ₁ is not φ₁ for an AR(2) — part of each correlation is inherited from shorter lags.
φ₂ is negative when ρ₂ < ρ₁², even with both correlations positive.
r₂ = r₁² is the signature of an AR(1), and makes φ̂₂ come out zero.
An AR(2) needs all THREE stationarity conditions; |φ₁| < 1 is neither necessary nor sufficient.
φ₁ + φ₂ = 1 means a unit root — no ACF at all, so difference first.
Differencing flips the sign: (1 − 0.6B − 0.4B²) gives Δyₜ = −0.4Δyₜ₋₁ + εₜ, so the ACF is (−0.4)ᵏ.
The PACF cuts off for an AR; the ACF cuts off for an MA.
For an AR(1) with negative φ, even lags of the ACF are positive.

lesson.title: Autocovariance of AR Processes
objectives: Derive the AR(1) variance and autocorrelation function from the model equation.
State and apply γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) and ρₖ = φᵏ.
Derive ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) for an AR(2) using the symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ.
Run the recursion ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂ from its two starting values.
Use the closed-form AR(2) variance and read its sign as a stationarity check.
Say why only the k = 0 equation carries σ² and why autocorrelations do not.
traps: ρ₁ = φ₁ holds for an AR(1) only; for an AR(2) it is φ₁/(1 − φ₂).
Only the k = 0 equation carries σ² — the recursion for k ≥ 1 is homogeneous.
E(yₜεₜ) = σ², not zero. Forgetting it loses the variance entirely.
The variance depends on φ², so its value is the same at φ and −φ.
Autocorrelations never involve σ²; the variance always does.
An oscillating ACF means complex roots, not an MA component.
γ₋₁ = γ₁ by symmetry — the AR(2) derivation fails without it.
A negative variance from the formula means the coefficients are outside the triangle.

lesson.title: Unit Roots, Differencing and ARIMA
objectives: Define a unit root three equivalent ways and say what it costs a model.
Compute the mean, variance and ACF of a random walk with drift and recognise the diagnostic signature.
Factor the difference operator out of an AR polynomial and identify the differenced model with the correct sign.
Use ARIMA(p, d, q) notation and determine d.
State and apply the invertibility condition, classifying a process as stationary, invertible, both or neither.
Say what the Dickey–Fuller test tests, which hypothesis is its null, and why its critical values are not the t values.
traps: A unit root means the coefficients sum to exactly 1 — add them first.
A random walk's variance is tσ²ε and grows; with drift the mean is μt and grows too.
The d in ARIMA(p, d, q) is the MIDDLE number — an ARIMA(2,1,0) needs ONE differencing.
The sign of the differenced model comes from the factorisation, not from the original equation.
The Dickey–Fuller NULL is the unit root, so failing to reject means difference the series.
Dickey–Fuller critical values are more negative than t values; a t table rejects too readily.
A finite MA process is always stationary — only invertibility can fail.
Over-differencing introduces an MA unit root and negative lag-1 autocorrelation.

topics.name: Random walk with and without drift

lesson.title: Random Walk With and Without Drift
objectives: Derive E(yₜ) = tμ and Var(yₜ) = tσ² by unrolling the recursion.
Derive Cov(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = tσ² and Corr = √(t/(t+k)), and name the condition violated.
State the three conditions for weak stationarity and when they give strict stationarity.
Separate trend-stationary from difference-stationary and choose the right repair.
Say what over-differencing produces and why an MA coefficient of 1 is awkward.
Identify a random walk as ARIMA(0, 1, 0) and explain the permanence of its shocks.
traps: Both the mean and the variance grow: tμ and tσ². Options with one constant are the traps.
Without drift the mean is constant at 0 but the variance is still tσ² — still non-stationary.
Corr(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = √(t/(t+k)) depends on t, not on the lag alone.
A shock in a random walk is PERMANENT, not geometrically decaying — that is the stationary AR(1).
yₜ = 5 + 0.2t + εₜ is trend-stationary: de-trend it, do not difference it.
Over-differencing gives a NON-INVERTIBLE MA component with θ = 1, not a better model.
Weak stationarity needs the autocovariance to depend on the lag ONLY.
Weak implies strict only for a Gaussian process.

lesson.title: Spectral Density and the Periodogram
objectives: State that the spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance function.
Use ∫f(ω)dω = γ₀ as a check on any spectral computation.
Give the white-noise, AR(1) and MA(1) densities and say where each keeps its variance.
State the MA sign convention in use and what changes under the other one.
Say why the periodogram is asymptotically unbiased yet inconsistent.
Explain what smoothing windows do, name three, and describe the bias–variance trade-off.
traps: The periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but NOT consistent — its variance does not shrink with n.
Consistency needs SMOOTHING, not merely a larger sample.
The spectral density transforms the AUTOCOVARIANCE function, not the residuals or the PACF.
∫f(ω)dω = γ₀, the variance — not 1, not the mean.
An AR(1) with φ > 0 peaks at LOW frequencies; only φ < 0 moves the mass to high frequencies.
The MA(1) density depends on the sign convention: 1.49 − 1.4cos ω under the minus convention.
Bartlett, Tukey–Hanning and Parzen are spectral windows, not tests and not models.
The cumulative periodogram tests WHITE NOISE, not stationarity or invertibility.

lesson.title: Components, Moving Averages and Smoothing
objectives: Name the four classical components and distinguish seasonal from cyclical.
Choose between additive and multiplicative decomposition from the data's behaviour.
Build a 2×k centred moving average, with its weights and term count.
Extract and normalise seasonal figures in additive and multiplicative form.
Give the exponential smoothing weights with their sum, half-life and average age.
State the ARIMA equivalences and the Slutsky–Yule result ρⱼ = (k−j)/k.
traps: A k-term moving average INDUCES ρⱼ = (k−j)/k in white noise — a smoothed cycle may be an artefact.
A 2×12 filter has THIRTEEN terms, with unequal end weights of 1/24.
Additive seasonal deviations sum to 0; multiplicative indices average to 1. Do not mix them.
The normalisation step at the end of a decomposition is the one most often omitted.
SES corresponds to θ = 1 − α, not θ = α.
SES gives a FLAT forecast at every horizon — correct for a random walk, wrong for a trend.
Seasonal has a known fixed period; cyclical does not. They are not interchangeable.
Detrend before averaging by season, not the other way round.

lesson.title: Ergodicity
objectives: Define ergodicity for the mean and give the equivalent condition Var(ȳₙ) → 0.
Write down the exact variance of the sample mean and explain the (1 − k/n) weights.
State the sufficient condition γₖ → 0 and say why decaying memory is what matters.
Compute the long-run variance and effective sample size for an AR(1) and an MA(1).
Produce the standard non-ergodic counterexample and verify it is stationary.
Explain why no standard-error correction can rescue non-ergodic data.
traps: Stationary does NOT imply ergodic — yₜ = Z + εₜ is the counterexample.
γₖ → 0 is sufficient, not necessary, so its failure does not prove non-ergodicity.
Negative autocorrelation IMPROVES the precision of the mean: n_eff = 9n at φ = −0.8.
Specify the baseline: the factor over σ²/n is 1/(1−φ)², over γ₀/n it is (1+φ)/(1−φ).
Ergodicity cannot be established from a finite sample — it is an assumption about the mechanism.
A random walk is not stationary, so the ergodicity question does not arise for it.
No standard-error correction fixes non-ergodic data; the estimator is inconsistent, not merely imprecise.
Ergodicity for the mean does not give ergodicity for second moments — they are separate.

topics.name: General linear process and Wold decomposition

lesson.title: General Linear Process and Wold Decomposition
objectives: Write the general linear process with ψ₀ = 1 and Σψⱼ² < ∞ and justify both conditions.
Compute γₖ as the overlap σ²Σψⱼψⱼ₊ₖ for AR, MA and ARMA processes.
Give the ψ weights of an AR(1), an MA(q) and an ARMA(1,1).
Distinguish Σψⱼ² from Σψⱼ and say what each measures.
State the Wold decomposition including its deterministic component.
Explain why the shocks are only uncorrelated, and why finite ARMA models remain needed.
traps: The Wold shocks are UNCORRELATED, not independent — the theorem is about linear structure only.
Σψⱼ² scaled by σ² is the variance; Σψⱼ is the long-run multiplier. They are different numbers.
A random walk is NOT a general linear process: ψⱼ = 1 gives a divergent Σψⱼ².
The theorem is an existence result and does not construct the weights.
It does not make finite ARMA models unnecessary — it makes them necessary.
ψ₀ = 1 is a normalisation, without which ψ and σ are not separately identified.
An ARMA(1,1) with φ = θ is white noise — a shared root cancels.
The sum is ONE-SIDED: past and present shocks only, never future ones.

topics.name: Forecasting with stationary and invertible processes

lesson.title: Forecasting Stationary and Invertible Processes
objectives: State that the minimum-MSE forecast is the conditional expectation, and when the median differs.
Derive the forecast and its error variance by splitting the weight representation at the horizon.
Give the AR(1) forecast and error variance, and the MA(q) q-step cut-off.
Say why the one-step error variance is σ² for any model with ψ₀ = 1.
Construct a prediction interval that widens correctly and say what it understates.
Explain why forecasting requires invertibility, and contrast with the random walk.
traps: The forecast error variance rises to γ₀ and stops — unbounded growth is the non-stationary case.
An MA(q) is forecastable for EXACTLY q steps, no more.
The one-step error variance is σ² for any model — no model beats that floor.
A forecast interval must WIDEN with the horizon, except for white noise.
A long-horizon forecast equalling the mean confirms the model rather than refuting it.
Intervals understate uncertainty, since the parameters are estimated and not known.
Forecasting needs invertibility — otherwise εₜ cannot be computed from the data.
For an AR(2) with complex roots the forecast OSCILLATES about the mean; that is correct.

lesson.title: Rank, Nullity, Sylvester and Frobenius
objectives: Give the equivalent definitions of rank and the bound rank ≤ min(m, n).
Apply rank–nullity with the column count, in both directions.
Read a rank off structure rather than by row reduction, including rows in arithmetic progression.
State Sylvester's rank inequality and convert it into bounds on the nullity of a product.
Use rank = trace for idempotent matrices to find the ranks a linear model needs.
Explain why rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) decides estimability.
traps: rank + nullity = number of COLUMNS, not rows.
The upper bound on υ(AB) is υ(A) + υ(B), with no −n. Test it on A = B = I.
In Sylvester's inequality the dimension subtracted is the SHARED one — columns of A, rows of B.
rank = trace holds only for IDEMPOTENT matrices; the Q26 matrix has trace 15 and rank 2.
Rows in arithmetic progression cap the rank at 2 for every size — do not row-reduce and lose it.
A non-zero skew-symmetric matrix cannot have odd rank.
The nullity of I − X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is k, not n − k; its RANK is n − k.
A Sylvester bound is only the answer to a 'minimum possible' question if it is attainable — check by construction, since random examples sit at the top of the range.

lesson.title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, Diagonalisation and Cayley–Hamilton
objectives: Compute eigenvalues from the characteristic equation.
Find eigenspaces by solving (A−λI)v=0.
Use algebraic and geometric multiplicities to decide diagonalisation.
Apply the spectral theorem to real symmetric matrices.
Use Cayley–Hamilton to reduce powers and obtain inverses.
traps: The zero vector is not an eigenvector.
Trace is the sum and determinant the product of eigenvalues, counting multiplicity.
Repeated eigenvalues do not automatically prevent diagonalisation.
Geometric multiplicity never exceeds algebraic multiplicity.
Orthogonal diagonalisation is guaranteed for real symmetric matrices, not all matrices.
In Cayley–Hamilton, the constant term multiplies I.
An inverse formula requires a non-zero determinant.

lesson.title: Quadratic Forms, Definiteness, Canonical Reduction and Inertia
objectives: Represent a quadratic form as xᵀAx with A symmetric.
Classify positive/negative definite, semidefinite and indefinite forms using eigenvalues.
Apply Sylvester's criterion using leading principal minors.
Reduce real symmetric forms to canonical diagonal form.
Use Sylvester's law of inertia under nonsingular congruence.
traps: The off-diagonal coefficient is half the displayed cross-term coefficient.
A positive determinant alone does not imply positive definiteness.
Strict Sylvester criterion uses leading principal minors, not all minors.
For semidefinite tests, all principal minors matter; do not merely replace > by ≥ in the strict test.
Zero eigenvalues rule out strict definiteness.
Inertia is invariant under nonsingular congruence, not arbitrary singular transformations.

lesson.title: Sequences, Series and Power Series
objectives: Find a radius of convergence by the ratio test and by the root test.
Recognise the coefficient patterns that give radius ∞, 0 and 1.
Substitute and test both endpoints, producing the correct bracket pattern.
Use the p-series boundary, the alternating series test, geometric and telescoping sums.
Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence and say where each can occur.
State the nᵗʰ-term test in the one direction that is valid.
