traps: The radius gives the OPEN interval; the endpoints must be tested separately.
Terms tending to zero does NOT imply convergence — the harmonic series is the counterexample.
Σ1/nᵖ needs p > 1 strictly; p ≥ 1 and p > 0 are both wrong.
R = lim |aₙ/aₙ₊₁|, not the other way up: growing coefficients give a SMALL radius.
The harmonic series diverges; it is the ALTERNATING harmonic series that sums to ln 2.
Σ1/(n(n+1)) = 1, while Σ1/n² = π²/6 — different series, and a favourite distractor pair.
The two endpoints of one series can behave differently, because they differ in sign pattern.
An absolute value in the series, as in Q28, changes the symmetry and the endpoint test but not the radius.

lesson.title: Continuity, Differentiability, Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorems
objectives: Test continuity at a point using two-sided limits and the assigned value.
Compute derivatives from first principles and compare one-sided derivatives.
Explain why differentiability implies continuity but not conversely.
Apply Rolle's theorem and Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem with all hypotheses checked.
State and use Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem.
traps: Continuity requires the limit to equal the assigned function value.
Differentiability implies continuity, but not conversely.
Rolle requires equal endpoint values and differentiability only in the open interval.
MVT guarantees at least one c, not necessarily a unique one.
If a hypothesis fails, the theorem is unavailable; its conclusion is not automatically false.
For piecewise continuity, compare left limit, right limit and f(a).

lesson.title: Maxima, Minima and Local Extrema
objectives: Identify critical numbers and stationary points.
Apply Fermat's theorem as a necessary condition.
Classify local extrema using first and second derivative tests.
Recognise stationary points that are not extrema.
Find absolute extrema on closed intervals by checking endpoints and interior candidates.
traps: f′(c)=0 is necessary at a differentiable interior extremum, not sufficient.
A critical point may have derivative undefined but still be an extremum.
x³ has a stationary point at zero but no extremum.
f′′(c)=0 makes the second derivative test inconclusive.
Absolute extrema on a closed interval may occur at endpoints.
The Extreme Value Theorem needs continuity on a closed bounded interval.

lesson.title: Riemann Integration and Improper Integrals
objectives: Explain Riemann sums and standard integrability criteria.
Evaluate definite integrals using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Define improper integrals through limits at infinite or singular endpoints.
Apply p-integral convergence criteria at zero and infinity.
Use comparison tests and split at interior singularities.
traps: A function tending to zero does not guarantee convergence.
At infinity, ∫₁∞x⁻ᵖ converges for p>1.
At zero, ∫₀¹x⁻ᵖ converges for p<1.
An interior singularity requires two one-sided limits.
An antiderivative does not replace the limit.
Riemann integrability requires boundedness.

lesson.title: Generalized Inverses, Moore–Penrose Inverse and Estimability
objectives: Define generalized and reflexive generalized inverses.
State and apply the four Moore–Penrose equations.
Use full-column-rank and full-row-rank formulas.
Interpret AA⁺ and A⁺A as orthogonal projections.
Determine estimability using row-space and null-space criteria.
traps: AGA=A alone does not define the unique Moore–Penrose inverse.
The full-column-rank and full-row-rank formulas are different.
Do not use (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ unless A has full column rank.
AA⁺ projects onto Col(A); A⁺A projects onto Row(A).
Rank-deficient coefficients may be non-unique even when fitted values are unique.
cᵀβ is estimable iff c lies in Row(X), equivalently is orthogonal to Null(X).

topics.name: Taylor's theorem, L'Hôpital's rule, uniform continuity

lesson.title: Taylor's Theorem, L'Hôpital's Rule and Uniform Continuity
objectives: Construct Taylor and Maclaurin polynomials.
Use the Lagrange remainder to bound approximation error.
Apply L'Hôpital's rule to valid 0/0 and ∞/∞ forms.
Rewrite other indeterminate forms before applying limit rules.
Distinguish pointwise continuity from uniform continuity.
traps: Taylor polynomial does not automatically equal the function globally.
A remainder bound requires a bound on the next derivative.
L'Hôpital applies directly only to 0/0 and ∞/∞ forms.
Products and differences need rewriting before L'Hôpital.
Uniform continuity requires one δ for the entire domain.
Continuous on a compact interval implies uniformly continuous, but continuous on an unbounded domain need not be.

topics.name: Functions of two variables: partial and total derivatives

lesson.title: Functions of Two Variables: Partial and Total Derivatives
objectives: Compute first and second partial derivatives.
Apply equality of mixed partials under continuity conditions.
Use total differentials and the multivariable chain rule.
Compute gradients and directional derivatives.
Interpret gradient magnitude and direction geometrically.
traps: In fₓ, hold y fixed; in fᵧ, hold x fixed.
A partial derivative is not the total derivative when both inputs vary.
Use a unit vector for the directional derivative.
Equality of mixed partials needs continuity conditions.
Existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee differentiability.
The gradient magnitude is the maximum directional derivative.

lesson.title: Saddle Points and Lagrange Multipliers
objectives: Find unconstrained stationary points using the gradient.
Classify non-degenerate stationary points using the Hessian determinant.
Recognise saddle points and inconclusive Hessian cases.
Set up equality-constrained optimisation using Lagrange multipliers.
Evaluate feasible candidates to identify constrained extrema.
traps: Solve both first partial equations before using the Hessian test.
D<0 means saddle, not a minimum.
D=0 is inconclusive.
For D>0, the sign of fₓₓ distinguishes minimum from maximum.
Lagrange equations produce candidates, not automatic global extrema.
Check regularity and exceptional constraint points.

topics.name: Double and triple integrals and their applications

lesson.title: Double and Triple Integrals, Change of Variables and Jacobians
objectives: Evaluate double integrals using Fubini's theorem.
Set correct limits for rectangular and non-rectangular regions.
Apply change of variables using the absolute Jacobian determinant.
Use polar coordinates to evaluate integrals over circular regions.
Evaluate triple integrals and interpret them as volume or mass.
traps: Draw the region before writing limits.
The polar area element is r dr dθ, not dr dθ.
Use the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant.
Transform the region and integrand as well as the area element.
An interior order reversal changes limits, not the region.
A triple integral of one gives volume, not surface area.

topics.name: Vector spaces, basis, dimension, row and column space

lesson.title: Vector Spaces, Subspaces, Span, Basis and Dimension
objectives: Apply the subspace test to subsets of vector spaces.
Compute and interpret the span of a set of vectors.
Test linear independence using linear combinations or rank.
Identify bases and compute dimensions.
Use the dimension formula for sums and intersections of subspaces.
traps: A subspace must contain zero.
A non-homogeneous linear equation usually defines an affine set, not a subspace.
Span is always a subspace.
A basis must both span and be independent.
All bases of a finite-dimensional space have equal size.
The union of subspaces is not generally a subspace.

topics.name: Systems of linear equations and row reduced echelon form

lesson.title: Linear Systems, Consistency, Rank Criterion and RREF
objectives: Use elementary row operations to obtain echelon and reduced echelon forms.
Determine rank from pivot positions.
Apply the rank criterion to test consistency.
Distinguish unique, infinite and no-solution cases.
Count free variables and describe homogeneous solution spaces.
traps: Compare rank(A) with rank([A|b]), not with the number of equations.
A pivot in the augmented column signals inconsistency.
A consistent system with rank below n has infinitely many solutions.
The number of free variables is n−rank(A), where n is the number of unknowns.
Homogeneous systems are always consistent.
Elementary row operations preserve the solution set.

lesson.title: Gram–Schmidt, Orthogonality and Orthogonal Matrices
objectives: Compute inner products, norms and projections.
Apply Gram–Schmidt to an independent set.
Construct an orthonormal basis for a span.
Verify whether a square matrix is orthogonal.
Use norm, inner-product and determinant properties of orthogonal matrices.
traps: Projection denominator is u·u; it is one only when u is a unit vector.
Gram–Schmidt preserves span but changes the basis vectors.
Normalise only after orthogonalising.
Orthogonal means QᵀQ=I, not Qᵀ=Q.
Orthogonal matrices have determinant ±1.
A direction vector is not automatically unit length.

topics.name: Trace, determinant and inverse of a matrix

lesson.title: Trace, Determinant and Inverse of a Matrix
objectives: Compute trace and use its linear, cyclic and similarity properties.
Apply determinant rules for products, transposes, scalar multiples and inverses.
Decide invertibility using determinant and rank.
Compute 2×2 and general inverses using adjugates.
Apply inverse product and transpose identities.
traps: tr(AB)=tr(BA) does not imply AB=BA.
Trace cyclicity allows cyclic permutations, not arbitrary rearrangement of factors.
det(cA)=cⁿdet(A) for n×n A; it is not c det(A) unless n=1.
det(AB)=det(A)det(B), not det(A)+det(B).
(AB)⁻¹=B⁻¹A⁻¹; order reverses.
A singular matrix has no inverse; do not divide by zero determinant.
The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

lesson.title: Multivariate Normal Distribution: marginals, conditionals and block matrices
objectives: Recognise the multivariate normal distribution from its mean vector and covariance matrix.
Obtain marginal distributions by selecting the corresponding mean entries and covariance submatrix.
Derive conditional means and covariance matrices using block-matrix partitioning.
Apply the Schur complement to calculate conditional covariance.
Distinguish zero correlation from conditional independence, using the joint-normal assumption correctly.
traps: A marginal distribution uses a covariance submatrix; do not invert it.
A conditional distribution uses Σ₂₁Σ₁₁⁻¹ and the Schur complement Σ₂₂−Σ₂₁Σ₁₁⁻¹Σ₁₂.
The conditional covariance does not depend on the observed conditioning value.
Zero covariance implies independence for jointly multivariate normal subvectors, not for arbitrary distributions.
The order of the blocks matters: dimensions must conform throughout.

lesson.title: Partial and Multiple Correlation: isolate and combine relationships
objectives: Distinguish simple, partial and multiple correlation.
Calculate a first-order partial correlation by controlling one variable.
Interpret partial correlation as correlation between residualised variables.
Calculate the multiple correlation coefficient using the inverse predictor-correlation matrix.
Relate partial correlations to the precision matrix and identify common exam traps.
traps: A partial correlation controls specified variables; a simple correlation does not.
The first-order partial correlation is not r12−r13r23; it includes a denominator.
Multiple correlation is non-negative and measures association of one variable with a set of predictors.
R² is the squared multiple correlation; do not confuse R with R².
A zero partial correlation means no linear association after linear control, not necessarily full probabilistic independence.

lesson.title: Principal Component Analysis: directions, eigenvalues and explained variance
objectives: Explain PCA as successive orthogonal linear combinations that maximise variance.
Find principal-component directions from eigenvectors of a covariance or correlation matrix.
Calculate eigenvalues, explained variance and cumulative explained variance.
Interpret scores, loadings, scaling choices and repeated eigenvalues.
Solve the June 2026 Paper 2 Q2 equicorrelation problem.
traps: Eigenvectors give directions; eigenvalues give component variances.
PC1 is a direction, not necessarily one original variable.
PCA scores are uncorrelated, not generally independent.
Covariance PCA is scale-sensitive; correlation PCA standardises variables.
Explained variance divides by the sum of all eigenvalues.

lesson.title: Hotelling’s T²: multivariate mean testing and the F transformation
objectives: Explain why Hotelling’s T² extends the one-sample t test to a vector mean.
Compute the sample mean vector, unbiased covariance matrix and its inverse.
Evaluate T²=n(x̄−μ₀)′S⁻¹(x̄−μ₀) without losing cross-product terms.
Convert one-sample T² to an exact F statistic and identify both degrees of freedom.
Distinguish one-sample, paired and two-sample Hotelling procedures.
traps: For the one-sample statistic, use T²=n d′S⁻¹d; do not omit n.
Use the sample covariance with divisor n−1, not the maximum-likelihood divisor n, in the standard test.
The inverse covariance matrix is essential; separate univariate t statistics do not reproduce the joint test.
For one sample, F=(n−p)T²/[p(n−1)] with df (p,n−p).
For paired data, form difference vectors and apply the one-sample procedure.
Do not confuse the one-sample and pooled two-sample F transformations.

lesson.title: Wishart Distribution: the sampling distribution of a covariance matrix
objectives: Define the Wishart distribution as a distribution of a random sum of outer products.
Recognise the degrees of freedom and scale matrix in a Wishart representation.
Use independence and the addition property to combine independent Wishart matrices.
Apply whitening and linear transformations to identify Wishart distributions.
Connect the sample covariance matrix of a multivariate normal sample to a Wishart distribution.
traps: For n independent Np(0,Σ) vectors, the sum of outer products has Wishart degrees of freedom n.
The Wishart dimension p is the order of the random matrix, not the number of observations.
Independent Wishart matrices add degrees of freedom only when they share the same scale matrix.
Whitening by Σ⁻¹/² changes the scale matrix to I, not the matrix dimension.
For a normal sample, (n−1)S follows Wp(n−1,Σ), not Wp(n,Σ).
A Wishart matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite; it is positive definite with probability one when the degrees of freedom are sufficient under a nonsingular scale.

lesson.title: Canonical Correlation: relationships between two variable sets
objectives: Explain canonical correlation as the maximum correlation between linear combinations of two variable sets.
Partition a joint covariance matrix into within-set and cross-covariance blocks.
Compute canonical correlations using singular values of a standardized cross-covariance matrix.
Use eigenvalues to obtain squared canonical correlations and interpret the largest root.
Solve the June 2026 Paper 2 Q20 matrix problem.
traps: Canonical correlation is between two optimally weighted linear combinations, not necessarily one raw variable from each set.
Eigenvalues of C′C are squared canonical correlations; take square roots to report correlations.
Standardise the cross block using both within-set covariance matrices.
The number of nonzero roots cannot exceed min(p,q).
If both within-set blocks are identity matrices, canonical correlations are singular values of the cross block.
The first canonical pair maximises correlation; later pairs obey within-set uncorrelatedness constraints.

topics.name: MLE of mean vector and covariance

lesson.title: MLE of the Mean Vector and Covariance Matrix
objectives: Derive the multivariate normal likelihood.
Obtain the mean vector MLE as the sample mean vector.
Obtain the covariance MLE using divisor n.
Distinguish the MLE from unbiased sample covariance using n−1.
Compute both estimators and recognise rank constraints.
traps: The covariance MLE divides by n, not n−1.
The unbiased sample covariance divides by n−1; it is not the MLE.
When μ is unknown, centre observations at x̄, not zero.
Use outer products to retain cross-products.
The estimate is symmetric positive semidefinite.
The centred covariance rank is at most min(p,n−1); if n≤p it is singular.

lesson.title: Mahalanobis Distance, Discriminant Analysis and MANOVA
objectives: Calculate and interpret squared Mahalanobis distance.
Explain how covariance adjusts distance for scale and correlation.
Distinguish linear and quadratic discriminant analysis.
Explain the purpose of MANOVA and recognise its four common criteria.
traps: Use Σ⁻¹, not Σ, in the Mahalanobis quadratic form.
D² is squared distance; take a square root only when D is requested.
LDA assumes a common within-group covariance matrix.
QDA permits group-specific covariance matrices.
MANOVA tests group mean response vectors jointly.
A small Wilks' lambda is not itself a p-value.

lesson.title: Factor and Cluster Analysis
objectives: Explain the common-factor model and distinguish common variance from uniqueness.
Interpret loadings, communalities and uniquenesses.
Explain factor rotation and recognise varimax.
Distinguish factor analysis from principal component analysis.
Describe hierarchical and k-means clustering and common linkage rules.
traps: Factor analysis models shared covariance among variables; PCA explains total variance.
Communality is explained common variance; uniqueness is specific plus error variance.
For standardised variables in the usual orthogonal model, communality plus uniqueness equals one.
Varimax is orthogonal; oblique rotations permit correlated factors.
Single linkage uses minimum cross-cluster distance and can create chaining.
Complete linkage uses maximum; average linkage uses mean cross-cluster distance.
Ward's method minimises the increase in within-cluster sum of squares.
Standard k-means requires k in advance and is sensitive to initial centres, scale and outliers.

lesson.title: sort, rank, order, which and range
objectives: Predict sort(), order() and rank() outputs.
Use order() as a permutation to reorder vectors.
Interpret which() and distinguish positions from values.
Interpret range() and calculate statistical range.
Avoid one-based indexing, ties and missing-value traps.
traps: sort returns sorted values; order returns positions that arrange the vector.
rank returns ranks in original order, not sorted values.
which returns positions where TRUE, not matching values.
R vector positions are one-based.
range returns minimum and maximum, not their difference.
diff(range(x)) computes statistical range.
which.max returns the first maximum's position.
rank ties use average ranks by default.
sort removes NA by default; range propagates NA unless na.rm=TRUE; which omits NA conditions.

lesson.title: Loops, functions and return values
objectives: Trace for, while and repeat loops in R.
Distinguish break from next and identify loop termination.
Read function definitions, arguments and returned values.
Recognise implicit return of the last evaluated expression.
Solve output-tracing questions involving loops inside functions.
traps: A for loop iterates over values in its sequence.
1:n is unsafe for n=0; seq_len(n) or seq_along(x) is safer.
break exits the nearest loop; next skips the current iteration.
while tests its condition before each pass; repeat needs an explicit exit.
A loop does not automatically return the last loop-variable value.
A function implicitly returns its last evaluated expression if return() is not called.
return(value) exits the current function immediately.
Trace assignments sequentially; do not confuse printed output with a returned value.
A while loop must update state so its condition can eventually become FALSE.

lesson.title: Scoping Rules in R
objectives: Explain lexical scoping and environment parent chains.
Trace name lookup through local and enclosing environments.
Distinguish <- from <<-.
Explain function enclosing versus calling environments.
Explain closures and retained state in nested functions.
traps: R uses lexical scoping: lookup follows the function's creation environment, not simply its caller.
A local binding masks a same-named binding in a parent environment.
Ordinary <- inside a function creates or updates a binding in its current evaluation environment.
<<- searches enclosing environments for an existing binding and updates the first match.
If <<- finds no enclosing binding, it assigns in .GlobalEnv.
A closure combines a function with its enclosing environment.
The calling and enclosing environments are not interchangeable.
A nested function can retain access to an outer local binding after the outer call returns.
Lookup stops at the first environment containing the name.
A global binding may be masked by a nearer binding.

lesson.title: Matrices and matrix operators in R
objectives: Create matrices and predict column-wise filling.
Read dimensions and indexing.
Distinguish element-wise and matrix multiplication.
Use transpose, determinant, solve, diagonal and margin summaries.
traps: matrix() fills by column unless byrow=TRUE.
* is element-wise; %*% is matrix multiplication.
A[i,j] means row i, column j.
Matrix products require matching inner dimensions.
det() requires a square matrix.
solve(A,b) solves Ax=b.
Use drop=FALSE to preserve matrix dimensions.

lesson.title: Statement ordering and output tracing in R
objectives: Trace assignments and expressions in source order.
Follow conditional and loop control flow.
Distinguish printed output from returned values.
Compute final values using updated bindings.
traps: R normally evaluates statements in source order.
A later assignment changes the value used by later expressions.
Only the selected if/else branch executes.
break exits the nearest loop; next skips the current iteration.
Assignment does not automatically print a value.
Printed output and a function's returned value are different.

lesson.title: Summary functions and missing values (NA) in R
objectives: Use common summary functions such as sum, mean, median, min, max and range.
Recognise how NA affects summaries and how na.rm=TRUE changes results.
Distinguish length, sum(!is.na(x)) and complete-case counts.
Interpret logical summaries and missing-value tests.
Avoid common NA, NaN and Inf output traps.
traps: Most arithmetic summaries return NA when an input contains NA unless na.rm=TRUE is used.
na.rm=TRUE removes missing values for that calculation; it does not modify the original vector.
is.na(x) returns a logical vector; sum(is.na(x)) counts missing entries.
length(x) includes NA values.
sum(!is.na(x)) counts observed entries.
NaN is also treated as missing by is.na().
na.rm=TRUE does not remove Inf.
mean(x) and median(x) are different summaries.
range(x) returns two endpoints; diff(range(x)) gives the spread.

lesson.title: Lists, factors, display and formatting in R
objectives: Create and index lists, including nested elements.
Distinguish [ ], [[ ]] and $ extraction.
Understand factors, levels and ordered factors.
Interpret print, str, class, summary and formatting functions.
Recognise factor-code versus label and display-versus-data traps.
traps: A list can contain objects of different types and lengths.
x[i] returns a sublist; x[[i]] returns the element itself.
x$name is shorthand for extracting a named list element.
A factor stores integer codes plus levels; codes are not necessarily the printed labels.
factor() levels are ordered alphabetically by default unless levels are supplied.
ordered=TRUE creates an ordered factor with level order.
as.numeric(factor) returns internal codes, not the original numeric labels.
str() displays structure; class() reports class; levels() reports factor labels.
format() returns character strings for display; it does not change the underlying numeric object.

topics.name: Data frames, data input and output, graphics and plots

lesson.title: Data frames, data input/output, graphics and plots in R
objectives: Create and inspect data frames and select rows and columns.
Understand recycling and equal-length column requirements.
Read common data import and export functions.
Interpret plot(), hist(), boxplot(), barplot() and graphical arguments.
Distinguish plot types, axes, labels and graphical device output.
traps: A data frame is a list of variables with equal-length columns.
data.frame() may recycle shorter columns only when lengths are compatible, such as a divisor; otherwise it errors.
df[row,column] uses row first and column second.
df$var selects a column; df[ , 'var', drop=FALSE] can preserve a data-frame result.
read.csv() imports comma-separated data; write.csv() exports it.
read.table() is a general delimited text reader.
plot() is generic; output depends on object classes and method.
hist() displays a frequency distribution; boxplot() summarises median, quartiles and potential outliers.
barplot() displays bar heights; plot(type='l') draws lines.
Graphical labels use main, xlab and ylab; axes and limits can be controlled.

lesson.title: LaTeX and word-processing software for statistical documents
objectives: Recognise LaTeX source, commands, environments and document structure.
Distinguish inline and displayed mathematics.
Understand common mathematical and document commands.
Identify word-processor functions for styles, tables, references and page layout.
Choose suitable tools for reproducible statistical reports and collaboration.
traps: LaTeX is a typesetting system; .tex is source and PDF is a common compiled output.
A LaTeX document commonly uses documentclass, begin{document} and end{document}.
Inline mathematics uses \(...\); displayed mathematics uses \[...\] or equation environments.
Commands begin with a backslash; environments use begin and end.
A backslash command is not a word-processor toolbar action.
Word-processor styles provide consistent headings and support navigation and automatic tables of contents.
A citation manager helps organise sources and bibliographies; citation style must be applied consistently.
Track Changes records edits; comments support review and collaboration.
A spreadsheet is not a substitute for a word processor when preparing long-form reports.
PDF is a fixed-layout output; source files remain editable.

lesson.title: Horvitz–Thompson Estimation and Unequal Inclusion Probabilities
objectives: Define first- and second-order inclusion probabilities and distinguish them from draw probabilities.
Construct the Horvitz–Thompson estimator of a finite-population total.
Explain design-unbiasedness using indicator variables.
Compute and interpret the design variance and its unbiased estimator when pairwise inclusion probabilities are positive.
Diagnose when an unbiased variance estimator cannot be computed from the observed sample.
traps: The inclusion probability πᵢ is the probability that unit i appears in the final sample; it is not necessarily the probability of a particular draw sequence.
The HT estimator is a total estimator. Divide by N to estimate a population mean when N is known.
Design-unbiasedness does not mean every realised estimate equals the population total.
The variance estimator needs second-order inclusion probabilities πᵢⱼ; positive first-order probabilities alone are not enough.
If πᵢⱼ=0 for a pair, the usual unbiased HT variance estimator has an unavailable denominator and cannot estimate that pair's contribution.
An unbiased estimator of a nonnegative variance can itself be negative for a realised sample.

lesson.title: Stratified Sampling and Allocation
objectives: Construct stratified estimators of a population mean and total.
Calculate variance under independent SRSWOR within strata.
Distinguish proportional, equal and Neyman allocation.
Allocate a fixed sample under unequal stratum sizes and variability.
Explain how finite-population corrections and costs affect allocation.
traps: Use population shares W_h, not sample shares, in the combined mean.
Use the stratum-specific FPC 1−n_h/N_h.
Neyman allocation uses N_hS_h when unit costs are equal.
A stratum census has zero sampling variance.
Stratification does not guarantee a variance reduction for every partition.

lesson.title: Ratio and Regression Estimators
objectives: State and calculate ratio and regression estimators of a population mean.
Explain when proportional versus linear auxiliary relationships support each estimator.
Compute adjusted estimates using known population auxiliary means.
Interpret residual-based approximate variances under SRSWOR.
Explain why the ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased.
traps: Ratio estimation scales ȳ by X̄/x̄; regression adds b(X̄−x̄).
Do not reverse the sign in the regression adjustment.
A ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased in finite samples.
The ratio estimator is most plausible for a proportional near-origin relationship.
State the sampling design before quoting a variance approximation.

lesson.title: Cluster Sampling
objectives: Distinguish elements, clusters and primary sampling units.
Calculate one-stage cluster estimators of totals and means.
State design variance under SRSWOR of clusters.
Interpret ICC, design effect and effective sample size.
Explain operational benefits and precision limitations.
traps: The primary sampling unit is the cluster, not the individual.
One-stage sampling observes every element in selected clusters.
Use cluster totals in the total estimator.
DEFF≈1+(m−1)ρ is an approximation.
Cluster sampling can reduce field costs while reducing precision per interview.

lesson.title: Systematic Sampling
objectives: Construct a linear systematic sample from an ordered frame.
Calculate first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
Explain the restricted sample space compared with SRSWOR.
Calculate exact design variance by enumerating possible starts.
Diagnose periodicity and variance-estimation limitations.
traps: The random start is selected from 1,…,k in the standard linear design.
Equal first-order inclusion probabilities do not imply the same variance as SRS.
Only k systematic samples are possible when N=nk.
Many second-order inclusion probabilities are zero.
A periodic frame pattern aligned with k can be harmful.
A single sample generally cannot provide an unbiased design-based variance estimate.

lesson.title: PPS Schemes and Their Estimators
objectives: Distinguish PPS with and without replacement.
Calculate draw probabilities from size measures.
Construct Hansen–Hurwitz and Horvitz–Thompson estimators.
State the corresponding variance expressions and probability requirements.
Describe cumulative-total and Lahiri selection procedures.
traps: HH uses draw probabilities p_i and averages over draws.
HT uses final inclusion probabilities π_i under without-replacement designs.
PPSWR can select a unit more than once.
PPSWOR draw probabilities do not generally equal final inclusion probabilities.
Selection method names do not by themselves identify replacement status.

lesson.title: Two-Stage, Multistage and Double Sampling
objectives: Distinguish multistage selection from two-phase measurement.
Identify PSUs, SSUs and later-stage units.
Calculate overall inclusion probabilities from conditional probabilities.
Construct inverse-probability HT contributions.
Explain auxiliary information in double sampling.
traps: Stage describes a level of unit selection; phase describes a round of measurement.
Multiply successive conditional probabilities; do not add them.
A PSU is not necessarily the final observation unit.
Phase two is normally subsampled from phase one.
A survey can combine multistage selection and two-phase measurement.

lesson.title: Non-Sampling Errors
objectives: Distinguish sampling error from non-sampling error.
Classify coverage, nonresponse, measurement, processing and specification errors.
Distinguish unit nonresponse from item nonresponse.
Explain why census operations remain vulnerable to non-sampling errors.
Match quality interventions to error mechanisms.
traps: A census can have non-sampling errors.
Increasing sample size does not automatically remove nonresponse or measurement bias.
Unit and item nonresponse are different.
Response rate alone does not determine nonresponse bias.
A wrong code introduced after interview is a processing error.

topics.name: Nonnegative variance estimation, ordered and unordered estimators

lesson.title: Nonnegative Variance Estimation and Ordered/Unordered Estimators
objectives: Explain why an unbiased variance estimate may be negative.
State the SYG variance estimator and its nonnegativity condition.
Explain limitations caused by zero joint inclusion probabilities.
Calculate Des Raj's ordered estimator and its variance for n=2.
Calculate Murthy's unordered estimator and explain its efficiency rationale.
traps: An unbiased variance estimator can be negative in a realised sample.
SYG nonnegativity requires the pairwise coefficient condition; it is not automatic for every design.
The usual pairwise variance estimator requires positive π_ij for relevant pairs.
Des Raj is order-dependent; Murthy is order-independent for n=2.
Use initial selection probabilities p_i in the Des Raj and Murthy formulas as defined for the observed units.

topics.name: ANOVA tables and degrees of freedom

lesson.title: ANOVA Tables and Degrees of Freedom in Experimental Designs
objectives: Separate treatment, block and experimental error variation in a one-way and blocked experiment.
Construct the ANOVA table for a balanced completely randomised design and a randomised block design.
Derive and use the degrees-of-freedom identities for treatments, blocks, error and total.
Calculate correction factor, total, treatment and residual sums of squares from treatment totals.
Form mean squares and the appropriate F statistic, then state the conclusion without confusing statistical and practical significance.
traps: Degrees of freedom count independent pieces of information after estimating parameters; they are not the number of observations in each source.
Treatment SS is measured around the grand mean; within-group error SS is measured around each treatment mean.
In a balanced CRD with a treatments, N observations: treatment df=a−1, error df=N−a, total df=N−1.
In a complete RBD with a treatments and b blocks: treatment df=a−1, block df=b−1, error df=(a−1)(b−1), total df=ab−1.
The F statistic is MS treatment divided by MS error, not by SS error.
A significant treatment F says at least one treatment mean differs; it does not say every pair differs or that the effect is practically important.
Blocking removes predictable nuisance variation from the residual; it does not increase the number of treatment replications.

lesson.title: CRD, Randomised Block Design and Latin Square Design
objectives: Identify when a completely randomised, randomised block or Latin square design is appropriate.
Construct treatment allocation layouts and identify experimental units, treatments, blocks, rows and columns.
Compare the control of nuisance variation and replication structure across the three designs.
Calculate and interpret the ANOVA components and degrees of freedom for complete RBD and Latin square layouts.
Recognise the assumptions and limitations of Latin square designs, including equal numbers of treatments, rows and columns.
traps: CRD controls no explicit block source; it relies on randomisation to distribute nuisance variation across treatments.
RBD has one block factor and each block contains every treatment once.
A Latin square controls two blocking directions, not two treatment factors.
A p×p Latin square has p treatments, p rows and p columns; every treatment appears exactly once in every row and column.
Latin square error df is (p−1)(p−2), not p²−p.
Latin square treatment, row and column effects are assumed additive; treatment-by-row and treatment-by-column interactions are not separately estimated.
Randomisation of a Latin square must preserve the Latin property; arbitrary cell shuffling destroys the design.

lesson.title: Factorial Experiments: Main Effects and Interactions
objectives: Explain why factorial experiments study two or more factors simultaneously.
Construct and interpret treatment combinations in a 2² and 2³ factorial experiment.
Calculate main effects and interaction effects using marginal means and contrasts.
Partition the treatment sum of squares into orthogonal factorial components in a balanced replicated 2² experiment.
Distinguish replication, randomisation and interaction, and interpret interaction before marginal main effects.
traps: A factorial experiment studies all combinations of the selected factor levels; it is not merely several separate one-factor experiments.
A main effect is an average effect over the levels of the other factor(s).
An interaction means the effect of one factor changes across levels of another factor.
When interaction is substantial, report simple effects or cell means; a marginal main effect can hide different or reversed responses.
For a full 2^k factorial there are 2^k treatment combinations and 2^k−1 non-empty factorial effects.
Replication means independently applying the same treatment combination to multiple experimental units; repeated readings on one unit are not automatically independent replications.
Orthogonality of factorial contrasts in a balanced design does not remove the need for randomisation.

lesson.title: Balanced Incomplete Block Designs and Incidence Matrices
objectives: Define BIBD parameters v, b, r, k and λ.
Apply bk=vr and λ(v−1)=r(k−1).
Construct and interpret the v×b incidence matrix.
Verify NN′=(r−λ)I+λJ and pair concurrence.
Distinguish necessary parameter conditions from existence.
traps: Incomplete means k<v.
r counts blocks containing one treatment; k counts treatments per block.
λ counts blocks containing a fixed pair, not one treatment.
bk=vr counts placements in two ways.
λ(v−1)=r(k−1) fixes one treatment and counts its partners.
With treatment rows, NN′=(r−λ)I+λJ.
Integer identities are necessary, not sufficient, for existence.

lesson.title: Principles of Experimental Design
objectives: Explain the principles of replication, randomisation and local control.
Distinguish experimental units, treatments, factors, blocks and replicates.
Explain how randomisation supports unbiased inference and valid error assessment.
Use local control/blocking to reduce nuisance variation.
Select CRD, RBD or Latin square according to the nuisance structure.
traps: Replication means independent experimental units receiving the same treatment, not repeated readings on one unit.
Randomisation is used to protect against systematic allocation bias and justify probability-based error assessment.
Local control reduces nuisance variation by grouping similar units into blocks.
Blocking is not the same as replication: a block controls a nuisance source; replication supplies repeated treatment applications.
CRD uses no blocking; RBD controls one major nuisance direction; Latin square controls two orthogonal directions.
Randomisation does not guarantee equal group sizes or remove all confounding by itself.
A design principle is not a specific layout: replication, randomisation and local control work together.

lesson.title: Confounding, Split-Plot Designs and PBIBD
objectives: Explain complete and partial confounding of factorial effects with blocks.
Identify which factorial effect is confounded with blocks in a specified layout.
Explain split-plot randomisation, whole plots and subplots.
Use the correct whole-plot and subplot error strata for tests.
Distinguish PBIBD from BIBD using associate classes and concurrence numbers.
traps: Confounding means a treatment effect cannot be separated from a block effect in that arrangement; it is not ordinary random error.
In a 2³ design split into two blocks of four, one 1-df factorial effect can be confounded with blocks.
Partial confounding rotates the confounded effect across replications so every effect can be estimated from some replications.
Split-plot randomisation is restricted: whole-plot treatments are randomised to whole plots, then subplot treatments within each whole plot.
The whole-plot factor is tested against whole-plot error; subplot factor and interaction use subplot error in the standard balanced split-plot ANOVA.
PBIBD pairs are divided into associate classes with different concurrence numbers λ₁, λ₂, …; not all pairs need occur equally often.
PBIBD is not simply a BIBD with unequal block sizes; its balance is defined through association classes.

lesson.title: Missing Plot Technique in Block Designs
objectives: Explain why missing plot values complicate block-design analysis.
Apply the one-missing-value estimator in a randomised block design.
Apply the one-missing-value estimator in a Latin square design.
Recalculate sums of squares and adjust error degrees of freedom after estimation.
Recognise limitations of simple missing-value formulas and the need for iterative methods with multiple omissions.
traps: In the RBD formula, t is number of treatments and r is number of blocks/replications; do not swap them.
Use treatment, block and grand totals calculated without the missing observation.
In a Latin square, the row, column and treatment totals all exclude the missing value.
After estimating one missing value, the error degrees of freedom are reduced by one.
The estimated value is a model-based completion for ANOVA, not a recovered observation.
With multiple missing values, estimates are generally simultaneous or iterative; do not apply a one-missing formula independently without checking dependencies.
Missingness related to the unobserved response can bias the analysis; the classical formula assumes the design model remains appropriate.

topics.name: Connectedness and orthogonality of block designs

lesson.title: Connectedness and Orthogonality of Block Designs
objectives: Define connectedness of a block design in terms of estimable treatment contrasts.
Use the treatment concurrence graph to reason about connectedness.
Interpret the information matrix C=R−NK⁻¹N′ and the rank condition rank(C)=v−1.
Explain orthogonality of treatment and block contrasts in complete block and Latin-square layouts.
Distinguish connectedness, balance and orthogonality.
traps: Connectedness means every treatment contrast is estimable after eliminating block effects; it is not the same as equal pair concurrence.
For a design with v treatments, rank(C)=v−1 is the connectedness condition when C=R−NK⁻¹N′.
A disconnected design can still estimate contrasts within each connected component, but not all contrasts across components.
A connected design need not be a BIBD; connectedness is about estimability, balance is about equal replication/concurrence.
Orthogonality means the relevant centred contrast cross-products are zero; it is not synonymous with connectedness.
In a complete RBD, every treatment occurs once in each block, making treatment and block contrasts orthogonal.
In a Latin square, treatment contrasts are orthogonal to both row and column contrasts under the standard balanced layout.

lesson.title: The Indian Statistical System: MoSPI, NSO and the NSC
objectives: Name MoSPI's two wings and say what each is responsible for.
Place the NSS, the CSO and the 2019 merger into the NSO on a timeline, with the correct years.
State how the NSC was created, who sits on it, and why non-statutory is the word that matters.
Attach each major release — national accounts, IIP, CPI, CPI-IW, WPI, PLFS, the Census — to the body that produces it.
Quote the current base years of GDP, CPI and IIP and the dates they changed.
Decide which body a given task belongs to, including the tasks that fall outside MoSPI.
traps: The NSC is non-statutory: created by resolution, not by an Act, so it recommends and cannot compel.
The Census belongs to the Registrar General under the Ministry of Home Affairs, not to MoSPI.
The first National Sample Survey (1950) preceded the Central Statistical Organisation (1951).
CPI-IW is the Labour Bureau's and the WPI is the Office of the Economic Adviser's; only CPI R/U/C is the NSO's.
The NSO is a wing of MoSPI, not a ministry in its own right.
After February 2026 the CPI base is 2024 and GDP and IIP are on 2022-23; the old 2011-12 and 2012 bases are superseded.
MoSPI's second wing is examinable: ₹150 crore project threshold, ₹5 crore MPLADS entitlement.

lesson.title: Commissions and Committees of the Indian Statistical System
objectives: Name the four landmark reviews of the Indian statistical system with their chairs and years.
State what the Rangarajan Commission recommended and which recommendations were and were not implemented.
Put the five poverty estimation committees in order and say what each changed.
Distinguish the two Rangarajan bodies, and recognise Tendulkar in both of his roles.
State what the Collection of Statistics Act 2008 does and the three changes made by the 2017 amendment.
Trace the SCES to SCoS to dissolution sequence and say what it illustrates about non-statutory bodies.
traps: Two different Rangarajan bodies: the 2000–01 Commission on the statistical system and the 2012–14 poverty expert group.
The statutory apex body the Rangarajan Commission recommended was never enacted; the NSC exists by resolution.
Lakdawala (1993) kept the calorie basis; Tendulkar (2009) abandoned it.
SCES (2019) was renamed SCoS (2023), not the reverse; SCoS was dissolved in September 2024.
The 2017 amendment added nodal officers and changed jurisdiction; it did not change penalties or make the NSC statutory.
Suresh Tendulkar chaired the first NSC in 2006 as well as the 2009 poverty group.
The Bowley–Robertson year is given as 1933 in some sources and 1934 in others; learn the recommendation, not the year.

lesson.title: Indian Statisticians and Their Contributions
objectives: State what Mahalanobis founded, in which years, and the two methods that carry his name.
Attach the Cramér–Rao bound, Rao–Blackwell, the score test and orthogonal arrays to C. R. Rao, with his main honours.
Give R. C. Bose's contributions to design of experiments and his part in the disproof of Euler's conjecture.
Identify S. N. Roy with the union–intersection principle and the largest root test.
Place P. V. Sukhatme in agricultural and world food statistics, with his institutions and his book.
Attribute Basu's theorem and the Bhattacharyya bound, and keep the ISI distinct from the International Statistical Institute.
traps: Euler's conjecture was disproved by Bose, Shrikhande and Parker — not by any other ISI figure.
National Statistics Day marks Mahalanobis's birthday, not the founding of the ISI.
C. R. Rao is not V. K. R. V. Rao; the latter was an economist on the National Income Committee.
The Indian Statistical Institute and the International Statistical Institute are different bodies.
Interpenetrating subsamples and pilot surveys are Mahalanobis's; Sukhatme's surveys were agricultural and international.
The ISI became an Institute of National Importance in 1959, which is not its founding year.
The Mahalanobis distance is dated 1930 in some sources and 1936 in others; do not bet a mark on the year.

lesson.title: Major Surveys and Indices
objectives: Place the National Sample Survey and name the four surveys that now descend from it, with what each measures.
State what HCES measures, its two recent rounds, and the headline MPCE and food-share figures from 2023-24.
Give the PLFS reference periods and the four changes the January 2025 redesign made.
Give the base year, weights, producer and current status of the CPI, the WPI and the IIP.
Apply a linking factor in the right direction and say why a linked series is not fully comparable.
Locate an unfamiliar survey or index on the chain from survey to index to national accounts.
traps: CPI's base is calendar 2024; IIP's and WPI's is financial 2022-23.
WPI covers goods only and is produced by DPIIT, not MoSPI.
WPI and PPI series are published concurrently; do not infer WPI discontinuation from PPI availability.
The consumption round before 2022-23 is 2011-12; the 2017-18 round was withheld.
Water supply and sewerage is the new IIP sector; gas supply sits inside electricity.
The CPI linking factor is new over old, so it multiplies; the IIP factor is defined the other way round.
PLFS estimates from January 2025 are not casually comparable with earlier ones.
CPI weights come from HCES 2023-24, not from the 2022-23 round.

lesson.title: Census and Vital Statistics
objectives: Distinguish the census, the Civil Registration System and the Sample Registration System by what each measures and what each is used for.
Give the census's history, legal basis and organisation, and the full Census 2027 schedule with both reference moments.
State what the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2023 changed, and from when.
Explain the SRS dual record system and say why two independent records beat one register.
Quote India's current vital rates with their correct periods and denominators.
Compute TFR, GRR and NRR from age-specific fertility rates and read whether a population is replacing itself.
traps: 1872 is the first census; 1881 is the first synchronous one.
The census, the CRS and the SRS all sit under the RGI in the Ministry of Home Affairs, not MoSPI.
IMR is per 1,000 live births, not per 1,000 population; MMR is per 1,00,000 live births.
Census 2027 reference moments are distinct from enumerator fieldwork windows; consult the Gazette notification for each State/UT.
The SRS rests on no statute; the census has the Census Act 1948 and registration the RBD Act 1969.
The proportion of births that are female is 918/1918, not 918/1000.
A TFR below replacement does not mean the population is falling — population momentum.
CRS completeness is measured against SRS-based estimates, so it cannot justify retiring the SRS.

lesson.title: Mann–Whitney U test
objectives: Choose Mann–Whitney U for two independent ordinal-or-higher samples.
Pool observations and assign average ranks to ties.
Calculate both U statistics from pooled rank sums and verify their relationship.
State the null mean and variance, including the tie correction.
Interpret rejection without automatically claiming a median difference.
traps: Mann–Whitney is for independent groups; signed-rank is for paired observations.
Pool observations before ranking; do not rank groups separately.
U is not the rank sum R; subtract n(n+1)/2.
Tied observations receive average occupied ranks.
U₁+U₂=n₁n₂; this is not either individual U.
Rejection compares distributions generally; it is not always a median test.

lesson.title: Wilcoxon signed-rank and sign tests
objectives: Identify paired observations and construct differences in a stated direction.
Apply the sign test after omitting zero differences.
Apply Wilcoxon signed-rank by ranking absolute nonzero differences and restoring signs.
Calculate rank sums and the no-tie null moments.
Choose between the two tests using the symmetry assumption.
traps: Paired methods analyse within-pair differences; they are not for two unrelated groups.
Fix the subtraction order before interpreting positive and negative signs.
Zero differences are omitted from the effective sample size.
Sign test uses directions only; signed-rank also uses magnitude ranks.
Tied absolute differences receive average ranks.
Signed-rank's usual location interpretation needs symmetric differences; sign test does not.

lesson.title: Kruskal–Wallis and Friedman tests
objectives: Choose Kruskal–Wallis or Friedman from the sample design.
Calculate Kruskal–Wallis H from pooled group rank sums.
Apply the Kruskal–Wallis tie correction and degrees of freedom.
Rank treatments within blocks and calculate the Friedman statistic.
Interpret omnibus results and identify when post-hoc comparisons are required.
traps: Kruskal–Wallis: pool observations across independent groups before ranking.
Friedman: rank treatments within each block, not across all raw values.
Both tests use k−1 degrees of freedom in the common chi-square approximation.
A significant omnibus statistic does not identify which pair differs.
Kruskal–Wallis median interpretation needs similarly shaped distributions.
Apply tie corrections when ties occur; do not silently use no-tie formulas.

lesson.title: Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ
objectives: Rank two columns consistently, compute Σd² and check Σd = 0.
Apply ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)] and reproduce the June 2026 answer of 0.345455.
Use max Σd² = n(n² − 1)/3 and ρ = 1 − 2(Σd²/max) to place or check a result.
Compute Kendall's τ from concordant and discordant pairs.
Say why ρ equals Pearson's r on the ranks, and handle ties with midranks.
Explain why Pearson's r and ρ can differ sharply, and what the gap diagnoses.
traps: Σd = 0 ALWAYS — it cannot confirm the ranking, only catch a subtraction error.
Rank both columns in the SAME direction, or the sign flips.
The Σd² shortcut is NOT exact with ties — use Pearson's r on midranks.
Pearson's r and ρ can differ by a factor of two on the same data (0.717 against 0.345 here).
τ is usually SMALLER than ρ, not larger.
ρ ≈ 3τ/2 is a small-correlation rule and fails badly at strong association.
No rank correlation on three items can be significant at 5%; the floor is 1/3! = 0.167.
Both coefficients understate an underlying bivariate-normal r — they are not on r's scale.

lesson.title: Matching nonparametric tests to design
objectives: Classify a study as independent, paired, blocked or association-based.
Select Mann–Whitney, signed-rank or sign test for two-sample designs.
Select Kruskal–Wallis or Friedman for several groups or treatments.
Distinguish rank association, distributional fit and sequence randomness procedures.
Justify a test choice using its design and key assumptions.
traps: Mann–Whitney is independent; signed-rank and sign are paired.
Kruskal–Wallis is several independent groups; Friedman is several related treatments.
KS tests distributional fit or equality of distributions; runs tests sequence randomness.
Spearman and Kendall assess association, not group differences.
A significant omnibus result does not identify which pair differs.
Check symmetry before interpreting signed-rank as a median/location test.

lesson.title: Kolmogorov–Smirnov and runs tests
objectives: Construct the empirical distribution function and describe its properties.
Calculate one-sample and two-sample KS statistics as maximum CDF gaps.
State the continuity and parameter-specification cautions for classical KS inference.
Count runs and calculate their null expectation and variance.
Choose KS or runs from the research target and interpret the result.
traps: KS uses the maximum absolute CDF gap, not an average gap.
One-sample KS assumes a fully specified continuous reference CDF for standard critical values.
Estimated null parameters require an adjusted calibration.
Two-sample KS compares two independent empirical CDFs.
Runs tests sequence order, conditional on the two label counts.
Too few runs suggests clustering; too many suggests alternation.

topics.name: Empirical distribution function and its properties

lesson.title: Empirical distribution function and properties
objectives: Construct the empirical distribution function from a sample.
Describe monotonicity, right-continuity, limits and jump sizes, including ties.
Derive the pointwise expectation and variance of the empirical CDF.
Calculate empirical quantiles using the inverse-CDF convention.
State the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem and connect the EDF to KS testing.
traps: The definition uses Xᵢ≤x, not Xᵢ<x.
A tie of size m creates a jump m/n, not 1/n.
Fₙ is nondecreasing and right-continuous; it never decreases.
E[Fₙ(x)]=F(x), while Var[Fₙ(x)]=F(x){1−F(x)}/n.
Uniform convergence is stronger than pointwise convergence.
The inverse-CDF median convention for even n may differ from averaging the two middle values.

topics.name: Linear rank tests for location and scale

lesson.title: Linear rank tests for location and scale
objectives: Define a linear rank statistic using scores assigned to pooled ranks.
Relate Wilcoxon rank-sum scores to the Mann–Whitney U statistic.
Recognise alternative location score systems.
Distinguish Ansari–Bradley and Mood scale score patterns.
Select a location or scale test and state its assumptions and direction.
traps: A linear rank statistic is T=Σa(Rᵢ); the score function matters.
Wilcoxon rank sum uses a(r)=r; U subtracts n₁(n₁+1)/2.
Ansari–Bradley scores are high near the pooled centre.
Mood scores are high at the pooled extremes.
A scale test is not automatically a test of variance without its centre assumptions.
Interpret a large statistic using the score direction and sample label.
